0.title: Job: Where Were You?
0.overview:
The book of Job is the Bible's most sustained meditation on innocent suffering, and it is among the most daring books in all of Scripture. It dares to let a righteous man scream at God. It dares to declare that God's friends gave wrong answers. It dares to end without fully explaining why the righteous suffer. And it dares to declare — from the lips of a man on an ash heap, stripped of children, wealth, and health — I know that my Redeemer lives.

Job is a prosperous, blameless man in the land of Uz (probably Edom or the Transjordan), a patriarchal figure whose piety is unimpeachable. The prose prologue (chs. 1–2) gives the reader what Job himself never has: access to the heavenly council, where the Adversary (הַשָּׂטָן, ha-satan — the accuser, a title not yet a personal name) challenges God with a devastating question: 'Does Job fear God for nothing?' (1:9). God grants the Adversary permission to test Job, and the catastrophe descends in waves. Job loses his livestock, his servants, his children, and finally his health. He is left sitting among the ashes, scraping his sores with a potsherd.

The poetic core (chs. 3–42:6) is a great drama of protest, debate, and divine encounter. Job's three friends — Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar — arrive to comfort him and stay to condemn him. Their theology is not entirely wrong (Proverbs does teach a general connection between righteousness and flourishing), but they apply it with a mechanical precision that makes it a lie: since Job is suffering, he must have sinned. Job refuses their comfort and their accusation, insisting on his innocence and demanding a hearing before God. A fourth voice — the young Elihu (chs. 32–37) — enters to rebuke both Job and the friends, shifting the frame from retributive to educative theodicy and partially preparing the way for the divine speeches. Then God himself speaks from the whirlwind (chs. 38–41), not to explain Job's suffering but to overwhelm him with the glory, complexity, and purposefulness of the creation — and with his own sovereign majesty. Job's response is not resentment but worship: 'I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you' (42:5). The prose epilogue (42:7–17) restores Job's fortunes, vindicates his honest protest, and condemns the friends' confident orthodoxy.

Job is not primarily a book about suffering — it is a book about God. It asks not 'why do the righteous suffer?' but 'who is God, and can he be trusted when everything is taken away?' The answer it gives is not a philosophical solution but a person — the living God, the God who speaks, the God who is big enough to handle honest protest, and the God who ultimately vindicates his servant. Christopher Ash writes that 'the book of Job is structured so that the reader has the answer the sufferer does not — and yet the answer does not satisfy the sufferer's question, because the answer is not an explanation but a Person.'

Job is also, in its deepest structure, a book about Christ. The innocent sufferer on the ash heap, wrongly condemned, crying out in apparent abandonment, reaching for a vindicating Redeemer — the shape of Job's story is the shape of the gospel. The go'el of 19:25 is the Christological heart: the kinsman-redeemer who vindicates the wrongly condemned, who stands at the last upon the earth, who is seen by the sufferer even in his own flesh. We know his name. Job did not. But the faith is the same: I know that my Redeemer lives.

1.title: Does Job Fear God for No Reason?
1.text: <sup>1</sup>There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.<sup>2</sup>There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.<sup>3</sup>He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.<sup>4</sup>His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them.<sup>5</sup>And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.<sup>6</sup>Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"<sup>9</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason?<sup>10</sup>Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.<sup>11</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>12</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>14</sup>and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them,<sup>15</sup>and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>16</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>17</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>18</sup>While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house,<sup>19</sup>and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."<sup>20</sup>Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.<sup>21</sup>And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."<sup>22</sup>In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
1.overview: Job of Uz is blameless and upright, fears God and turns away from evil; he has seven sons, three daughters and great wealth, and he offers a burnt offering for each child in case they have cursed God in their hearts (vv. 1-5). In the council of heaven the LORD commends him to Satan, who answers, Does Job fear God for no reason? and predicts that without the hedge of blessing he will curse God to his face. The LORD puts all Job has into Satan's hand, but not Job himself (vv. 6-12). In one day four messengers report the loss of oxen and donkeys to Sabean raiders, of the sheep to fire from heaven, of the camels to Chaldean raiders, and of all ten children to a great wind (vv. 13-19). Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships: The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD. In all this he does not sin or charge God with wrong (vv. 20-22).
1.theology:
The book's question is whether God deserves to be loved for himself, or only for his gifts. Satan's word for no reason (chinnam) returns in God's mouth (2:3), in Job's (9:17) and in Eliphaz's (22:6). The Greek Old Testament renders it dorean, the word the New Testament uses of Christ hated without a cause (John 15:25) and of our justification as a gift (Rom 3:24).

God is sovereign over suffering without being the author of evil. Human wickedness, natural disaster and Satan's malice all act, and none acts outside God's permission and limit; the cross is the clearest instance of the same pattern (Acts 2:23; 4:27-28). To say the LORD has taken away is not sin; to charge him with wrong would be (v. 22).
1.examples:
God, not Satan, is the first to mention Job.

The Hebrew says "blessed" where the ESV rightly says "cursed" (vv. 5, 11), so Job's blessed be the name of the LORD answers Satan with his own word.

Job offered ten sacrifices after every feast; Christ offered one and sat down (Heb 10:11-12).

Four messengers, each cutting across the last, and the children last of all.

Five verbs of grief and worship in a single verse.

The book never says the children died for their sins.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Man in the Land of Uz
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job lives in Uz, outside Israel, and the narrator gives him four marks of true piety: blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil (v. 1). He has seven sons and three daughters and is the greatest of all the people of the east (vv. 2-3). When his children's feasts end he rises early and offers a burnt offering for each of them, in case they have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Scripture's verdict on Job comes before his trouble, so that no reader can explain the trouble by him. God himself repeats it (v. 8; 2:3).

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil.

The book begins like a story told at a fireside: there was a man. Uz lies outside Israel; Lamentations sets it with Edom (Lam 4:21), the country south-east of the Dead Sea. There is no mention anywhere in the book of Israel, Abraham, the covenant, the law or the temple. Job offers his own sacrifices as the head of his family, as the patriarchs did. We do not know who wrote the book or when. We do know Job was a real man: Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel as a byword for righteousness (Ezek 14:14), and James holds him up to Christians (James 5:11). His story is set outside Israel on purpose. It belongs to anyone who has ever suffered.

Then the verdict, in four parts. Blameless (Hebrew tam) means whole, all of a piece; its noun is the integrity that God will say Job still holds fast (2:3). Upright means straight in his dealings. He feared God, and that fear showed in what he did: he turned away from evil. It does not mean sinless. Job himself will ask God to pardon his transgression (7:21) and will speak of the iniquities of his youth (13:26). It means that there was no hidden life behind the visible one.

This matters for everything that follows. The narrator gives the verdict before a single blow falls, and God will repeat it word for word (v. 8; 2:3). Whatever explains Job's suffering, it will not be Job's sin. The reader is told that on the first line, so that he can never take the friends' side.

verseByVerse.quote: There were born to him seven sons and three daughters. He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There were born to him seven sons and three daughters. He possessed 7,000 sheep, 3,000 camels, 500 yoke of oxen, and 500 female donkeys, and very many servants, so that this man was the greatest of all the people of the east.

Seven and three make ten, and the flocks follow the same pattern as the children: seven thousand and three thousand, five hundred and five hundred. It is the storyteller's way of saying complete. Job had everything a man of his world could want, a full house and full fields. The people of the east were famous for their wealth and their wisdom; when Scripture wants to praise Solomon's wisdom, it says it surpassed theirs (1 Kgs 4:30). Job was the greatest of them.

Keep the list in mind. Every item on it is about to be taken, in the same order as it is given, with the children last. And at the end of the book the list will be read out again (42:12-13), with every number doubled but one.

verseByVerse.quote: His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, "It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts." Thus Job did continually.
verseByVerse.commentary:
His sons used to go and hold a feast in the house of each one on his day, and they would send and invite their three sisters to eat and drink with them. And when the days of the feast had run their course, Job would send and consecrate them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all.

A happy family. The brothers take turns to host, and they do not leave their sisters out. And their father watches over their souls. When each round of feasting ends, he calls them to make themselves ready, gets up early, and offers a burnt offering for every one of them: ten sacrifices.

For Job said, It may be that my children have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. He has no evidence. He offers for sins he cannot see, in hearts he cannot read. The Hebrew here actually says blessed God; scribes could not bear to write "curse God" and used the opposite word, and the ESV rightly translates the sense. The same word will come back in Satan's mouth (v. 11) and in Job's (v. 21), and it is the hinge of the chapter.

Thus Job did continually. Here is a good father, and a picture of the limit of every priest before Christ. He had to do it again after every feast, because no sacrifice he offered could finish the matter. Every priest stands daily at his service, offering repeatedly the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down (Heb 10:11-12). The Christian parent still prays for his children every day. He no longer has to wonder whether the sacrifice was enough.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heavenly beings present themselves before the LORD, and Satan comes among them (v. 6). The LORD speaks first: Have you considered my servant Job? (vv. 7-8). Satan answers with the question the whole book will test: Does Job fear God for no reason? Take away the hedge, and he will curse you to your face (vv. 9-11). The LORD puts everything Job has into Satan's hand, but not Job himself (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Satan is real and malicious, and he is on a leash. Nothing reaches Job that did not first pass through the council of God, and the limit is set before the first blow falls.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them.

The curtain goes up on a scene Job never sees. The sons of God are heavenly beings; the book uses the phrase again for the angels who shouted for joy when God laid the foundation of the earth (38:7). They come to present themselves, like officials reporting to a king, as the prophet Micaiah saw the LORD sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing beside him (1 Kgs 22:19).

In Hebrew Satan has the article: the satan, the accuser or adversary, as the ESV's footnote says. He appears in the same role in Zechariah, standing at his right hand to accuse him (Zech 3:1). Some read him here as a court official, a prosecutor doing an unpleasant job for God. But his aim in this chapter is that Job should curse God (v. 11), and that is not a servant's aim. The New Testament names him: that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the accuser of our brothers ... who accuses them day and night before our God (Rev 12:9-10). He is real, he is hostile, and he still has to come before the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD said to Satan, From where have you come? Satan answered the LORD and said, From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it.

God asks, not because he needs to know, but because Satan must give an account. And the answer is restless: to and fro, up and down. Peter uses the picture to warn Christians: Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Pet 5:8). He is not everywhere at once, and he is not idle. He has been looking at people.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to Satan, Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil?

Notice who raises Job's name. Not Satan: the LORD. Have you considered is literally "have you set your heart on". God points to Job the way a father points to a son he is proud of. My servant is the title Scripture gives to Abraham, Moses and David, and at last to the Servant of Isaiah who suffers for others (Isa 52:13). And God repeats the narrator's verdict, all four parts, and adds there is none like him on the earth.

This is an unsettling verse, and a deeply comforting one. Job's trouble does not begin with Job's failure. It begins with God's delight in him. That is not a rule for every suffering; much of our trouble we bring on ourselves, and Scripture says so. But it breaks the equation the friends will spend thirty chapters defending, that a man in pain must be a man in the wrong. Some sufferings begin in heaven, with God's pleasure in a servant he means to show to the world.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Does Job fear God for no reason? Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan answered the LORD and said, Does Job fear God for no reason?

Here is the question of the book. For no reason is one Hebrew word, chinnam: gratis, for nothing, without pay. Satan does not deny that Job is devout. He denies that Job's devotion is love. It is a wage, he says. Job serves God because God pays well.

Have you not put a hedge around him and his house and all that he has, on every side? You have blessed the work of his hands, and his possessions have increased in the land. Satan's own words admit that God has protected Job on every side. And his charge is aimed at God as much as at Job. If he is right, then God does not deserve to be loved for himself. He is loved only for what he hands out, and no one would stay with him if the gifts stopped.

Watch the word as the book goes on. God will use it back at Satan: you incited me against him to destroy him without reason (2:3). Job will use it, not knowing how true it is: he ... multiplies my wounds without cause (9:17). The Greek translation of the Old Testament renders it dorean, and the New Testament picks up the same word twice. Of Christ: They hated me without a cause (John 15:25). And of us: we are justified by his grace as a gift (Rom 3:24). The gospel is God giving for no reason in us, and the faith it creates loves him back the same way.

Every believer is asked Satan's question sooner or later, usually by a loss. What would be left of your faith if the hedge came down?

verseByVerse.quote: But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face." And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But stretch out your hand and touch all that he has, and he will curse you to your face. Satan does not ask to strike Job himself. He asks God to do it: stretch out your hand. And curse is again the Hebrew bless. Satan's prediction is that Job will "bless" God to his face, meaning the opposite. Keep that word for verse 21.

And the LORD said to Satan, Behold, all that he has is in your hand. Only against him do not stretch out your hand. So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD.

People sometimes call this a wager. It is not. A wager is made when the outcome is uncertain, and God has just said what Job is. It is a demonstration, before an audience in heaven, that God can be loved for himself. Paul says something like it of the church: that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places (Eph 3:10).

And there is a limit, set before a single blow falls: only against him do not stretch out your hand. Satan can go no further than he is allowed. Jesus told Peter the same thing on the night of his arrest: Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail (Luke 22:31-32). Job did not know about the council. The Christian knows that there is one, and that Jesus is in it, praying. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability (1 Cor 10:13).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On one ordinary day, while the children feast at the eldest brother's house, four servants arrive one on another's heels: raiders have taken the oxen and donkeys (vv. 13-15), fire from heaven has burned the sheep (v. 16), raiders have taken the camels (v. 17), and a great wind has brought the house down on all ten of Job's children (vv. 18-19). Each ends, I alone have escaped to tell you.
verseByVerse.theology: Wicked men, weather, and the devil behind them both; and over all of it, the permission of God. The book never lets any one of these explain the others away.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and there came a messenger to Job and said, "The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them, and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now there was a day when his sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house. The words echo verse 6: now there was a day. What was decided in heaven arrives on earth on an ordinary day, at a family meal. If the brothers hosted in order of age, the round of feasts had just begun again.

And there came a messenger to Job and said, The oxen were plowing and the donkeys feeding beside them, and the Sabeans fell upon them and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you.

Ordinary work: ploughing, grazing. Then raiders from Sheba in the south, men who kill for livestock. The first blow is plain human wickedness. The Sabeans were not puppets; they chose their raid and will answer for it. But they have come because God allowed it and Satan wanted it.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you." While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, The fire of God fell from heaven and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them, and I alone have escaped to tell you.

Probably lightning. But the servant calls it the fire of God, the phrase Israel used for the fire that fell at Elijah's word (2 Kgs 1:12). Even the messenger reads it as heaven turned against his master. That is how it looked from the ground, and Job will spend the rest of the book wrestling with exactly that appearance.

While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, The Chaldeans formed three groups and made a raid on the camels and took them and struck down the servants with the edge of the sword, and I alone have escaped to tell you. Raiders again, this time from the north-east, the direction of Mesopotamia. Men, then sky, then men. Trouble comes from every side and through every kind of cause. No one explanation will cover it, and Job is not given time to look for one: while he was yet speaking, three times over. He cannot take in one loss before the next arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, "Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
While he was yet speaking, there came another and said, Your sons and daughters were eating and drinking wine in their oldest brother's house, and behold, a great wind came across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead, and I alone have escaped to tell you.

The storyteller has kept the worst till last. Ten children, in one room, under one roof, at the very meal their father used to pray over. A wind from the desert struck the four corners, every side at once, and there was nowhere to run. By evening Job has ten graves to dig.

Two things must be said to any parent who reads this with a grave of his own. First, the book never says these children died for their sins. Bildad will say it (8:4), and the LORD will judge Bildad and his friends for speaking what is not right (42:7). Second, Job's prayers for them were not wasted. Nothing in the book suggests that a father who prays loses his children because his prayers failed. What the book does is refuse to explain the loss, and then show that God can be trusted in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–22 — The LORD Gave, and the LORD Has Taken Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job tears his robe, shaves his head, falls to the ground and worships (v. 20): Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD (v. 21). In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: Satan said Job would curse God to his face. Job blesses his name, using the same Hebrew word. The first round goes to God, and to the man who trusted him with nothing left in his hands.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head and fell on the ground and worshiped.

Five verbs. The first four are grief, and they are the grief of his time: the torn robe, the shaved head, the body thrown on the ground. Job does not pretend. There is no brave face and no pious calm. Then the fifth verb, in the same sentence: and worshiped. The word means he bowed down, face to the earth.

Grief and worship are not opposites. A Christian at a graveside does not have to choose between weeping and trusting. Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend (John 11:35), and Paul tells the church not to stop grieving but not to grieve as others do who have no hope (1 Thess 4:13). Tears are not unbelief. Job's were on the ground, and so was his worship.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he said, Naked I came from my mother's womb, and naked shall I return. He came with nothing and will leave with nothing; everything in between was loaned. The Preacher says the same (Eccl 5:15), and Paul: we brought nothing into the world, and we cannot take anything out of the world (1 Tim 6:7).

The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Job does not blame the Sabeans or the Chaldeans or the weather. He does not know about Satan. He goes straight past every second cause to the first one, and he is right to: God will say to Satan, you incited me against him (2:3). This is not fatalism. It is the conviction that his losses were not in the hands of chance. They were in the hands of the one who gave him everything in the first place.

Blessed be the name of the LORD. Here is the word Satan used. He said Job would "bless" God to his face, meaning curse. Job blesses God, and means it. The first round is over, and Satan's theory has failed in a single verb.

This verse is not a formula to recite over someone else's grief, and it was not easy for Job. He said it with his head shaved and his clothes torn, and in chapter 3 the same man will curse the day he was born. Both are in him. But it shows what a person can say from the bottom. Long afterwards another man was stripped, and soldiers divided his clothes among them (John 19:23-24). He had nothing left, and he did not curse God: Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46).

verseByVerse.quote: In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In all this Job did not sin or charge God with wrong.

Read the verdict carefully, because the rest of the book depends on it. Job said that the LORD had taken away his children, and the narrator says that was not sin. What Job did not do was charge God with wrong, accuse him of something unfitting. To say "God did this" is not sinful. To say "God did this and was wrong to" would be. The whole book lives between those two sentences.

And look at the scene from above. Satan, the Sabeans, the Chaldeans, the fire and the wind all had their part, and over it all stood the permission and purpose of God. The same pattern appears at the cross, where Peter says Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Wicked men did their worst, Satan entered Judas, and God's hand and plan had predestined it (Acts 4:28). If God could rule the darkest day in history for good, he rules yours.

Satan asked whether anyone would love God for no reason. One man did it perfectly. Jesus loved the Father with nothing in his hands and suffered without a cause, and because of him the accuser of our brothers has been thrown down (Rev 12:10). He is worthy of such love.

2.title: Skin for Skin
2.text: <sup>1</sup>Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."<sup>3</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."<sup>4</sup>Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life.<sup>5</sup>But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life."<sup>7</sup>So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.<sup>8</sup>And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.<sup>9</sup>Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."<sup>10</sup>But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.<sup>11</sup>Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.<sup>12</sup>And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.<sup>13</sup>And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
2.overview: The heavenly court meets again. The LORD repeats his verdict on Job and adds that he still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason. Satan answers, Skin for skin! and says Job will curse God if his body is touched; the LORD gives Job into his hand but forbids him to take his life (vv. 1-6). Satan strikes Job with loathsome sores from head to foot, and Job sits in the ashes scraping himself with a broken piece of pottery. His wife says, Curse God and die; he answers, Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?, and does not sin with his lips (vv. 7-10). Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar come to comfort him, do not recognize him, weep, and sit with him on the ground seven days and nights without a word (vv. 11-13).
2.theology:
God rules over evil without doing evil: Satan incites, and God says you incited me (v. 3), as 2 Samuel 24:1 and 1 Chronicles 21:1 describe one event from both sides. The limit on Satan moves, but it remains.

Job is struck with the very curse the law pronounces on the disobedient (Deut 28:35) though he has not disobeyed, so that every onlooker takes him for cursed. The Servant of Isaiah was esteemed stricken by God (Isa 53:4), and Christ became a curse for us (Gal 3:13).
2.examples:
The second time, Satan comes to present himself.

Job's wife turns God's own words, he still holds fast his integrity, into a taunt.

Job says she speaks like a foolish woman; he does not call her one.

The sores run from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head, as in Deuteronomy's curse.

Satan is not mentioned again after this chapter.

Seven days of silence: the friends' finest hour.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heavenly court meets again, and Satan comes to present himself before the LORD (vv. 1-2). The LORD repeats his verdict on Job and adds, He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason (v. 3). Satan answers, Skin for skin! Touch his body, and he will curse you to your face (vv. 4-5). The LORD gives Job himself into Satan's hand, only spare his life, and Satan goes out and strikes him with sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: God does not keep his distance from Job's suffering. He says to Satan, you incited me. The evil is Satan's; the permission, and the limit, are God's.

verseByVerse.quote: Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD. And the LORD said to Satan, "From where have you come?" Satan answered the LORD and said, "From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the LORD, and Satan also came among them to present himself before the LORD.

The scene repeats almost word for word, with one addition. In chapter 1 Satan simply came among them (1:6). Now he comes to present himself before the LORD, like the others. He has lost the first round, and he has to report. However much he roams the earth (v. 2), he cannot stay away from the throne. He answers to God, whether he likes it or not.

The same question and the same restless answer: From going to and fro on the earth, and from walking up and down on it. Nothing has changed for Satan. Everything has changed for Job, and he does not know why.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to Satan, Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on the earth, a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil? He still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to destroy him without reason.

God repeats his verdict and adds two things. First, he still holds fast his integrity. The word is the noun of blameless (1:1): Job is still whole. His children are dead and his wealth is gone, and he has not let go.

Second, and startling: you incited me against him. God does not say Satan did it while he looked away. He says Satan moved him. Readers of Samuel and Chronicles will know the verb. Samuel says the LORD incited David to number Israel (2 Sam 24:1); Chronicles says Satan ... incited David (1 Chr 21:1). Both are true. Satan means evil by it, and God rules over it for his own ends. God owns what happened to Job, and he does not let Satan off.

And without reason is Satan's word from 1:9, chinnam, handed back to him. There was nothing in Job that called for this. God himself says so. Whatever the friends are about to argue, the LORD has already ruled: this suffering was not deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Satan answered the LORD and said, "Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life. But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Satan answered the LORD and said, Skin for skin! All that a man has he will give for his life.

Skin for skin is a proverb, probably from trading: a man will give one hide to save another, and he will give anything to save his own. Satan's argument is that the first test did not go deep enough. Job lost his property and his children, but he still had himself. Touch that, and you will see what he really loves.

But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and he will curse you to your face. Again Satan asks God to do the striking, and again curse is the Hebrew bless. It is the cynic's creed, and it sounds shrewd: in the end everyone looks after number one. Satan has never met a love that would not save itself. He is about to watch one in Job, and one day he will watch it perfectly, in a man who saved others and would not save himself.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Satan, "Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life." So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the LORD said to Satan, Behold, he is in your hand; only spare his life. The limit moves, but there is still a limit. Satan may touch Job's body. He may not take his life. God draws the line before the blow, as he did the first time (1:12).

So Satan went out from the presence of the LORD and struck Job with loathsome sores from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head.

Here is something any Israelite reader would feel at once. The Hebrew for loathsome sores is the phrase the law uses for one of the curses on a disobedient people, and the ESV's wording of the rest of the sentence is word for word the same: The LORD will strike you ... with grievous boils of which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head (Deut 28:35). Job has not broken the covenant. But he looks exactly like a man who has. Everyone who sees him will draw the obvious conclusion, and three men are about to.

That is the pattern of the cross. The prophet says of the Servant, we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted (Isa 53:4). The onlookers were right that he bore a curse and wrong about whose. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Gal 3:13). Job bore the look of the curse without the guilt. Christ bore the curse itself, and it was ours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job sits in the ashes and scrapes his sores with a piece of broken pottery (v. 8). His wife says, Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die (v. 9). He answers, Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? In all this Job did not sin with his lips (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The body that Satan was sure would break is the place where Job holds on. The second round goes to God as well.

verseByVerse.quote: And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he took a piece of broken pottery with which to scrape himself while he sat in the ashes.

A shard from a broken pot, to scrape the itching and the running sores. It is one small picture, and it tells you how far he has fallen. The greatest man in the east sits in the ashes with a piece of rubbish in his hand. The Greek translation of the Old Testament puts him on the rubbish heap outside the town, where the beggars and the diseased were left; the Hebrew says only the ashes, which were also the place of mourning.

Jesus told of a poor man laid at a rich man's gate, covered with sores, and even the dogs came and licked his sores (Luke 16:20-21). God's people have often looked like that. And their Lord did not stay away from that place: Jesus also suffered outside the gate (Heb 13:12).

verseByVerse.quote: Then his wife said to him, "Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then his wife said to him, Do you still hold fast your integrity? Curse God and die.

Listen to her first question. It is God's own sentence from verse 3, he still holds fast his integrity, turned into a question. God said it with pride. She says it in despair, or scorn. The one thing God delights in is the one thing she wants him to let go of. And her advice is Satan's goal to the letter: curse God, again the Hebrew bless. Then die, and be done with it.

She has been hard judged, and she has earned some of it. But remember what she has lost. Ten children are in the ground; the wealth is gone; now she watches her husband scrape his sores in the ashes. Her words are the words of someone who thinks faith has failed and would rather see the suffering end in death than go on. Plenty of believers have heard those words from someone they love, or have said them to themselves. The book records her once and does not mention her again.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to her, "You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil?" In all this Job did not sin with his lips.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But he said to her, You speak as one of the foolish women would speak. The foolish person in Scripture is not the stupid one but the one who lives as if God does not matter: The fool says in his heart, There is no God (Ps 14:1). And notice how Job puts it. He does not call her a fool. He says she is talking like one. He rebukes the words and spares the woman.

Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? We: he takes her into the question with him. Evil here means calamity, not wickedness, as when God says, I make well-being and create calamity (Isa 45:7). Job has taken God's good gifts for years without asking whether he deserved them. Is he now to take only the good, and hand back the rest? His faith is not a contract that lapses when the payments stop.

In all this Job did not sin with his lips. In chapter 1 Job worried that his children had cursed God in their hearts (1:5). Here the narrator speaks of Job's lips, because the test was whether he would curse God aloud, to his face. And the mouth shows the heart: out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt 12:34). Satan has lost twice. He is not mentioned again in the book.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–13 — Seven Days on the Ground
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar hear of Job's trouble and arrange to come to show him sympathy and comfort him (v. 11). They do not recognize him; they weep aloud, tear their robes and throw dust toward heaven (v. 12). Then they sit with him on the ground seven days and seven nights without a word, for they saw that his suffering was very great (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: This is the best thing the friends do in the whole book. When they begin to speak, they begin to go wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite. They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now when Job's three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place, Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite.

They come from the lands around Edom and Arabia. Eliphaz shares his name with a son of Esau, whose own son was called Teman (Gen 36:10-11), and Teman was famous for its wise men: Is wisdom no more in Teman? (Jer 49:7). Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:2). Naamah is unknown. These are serious men from the wisdom country, and they come as friends.

They made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and comfort him. Their intentions were good. They took trouble, arranged to travel together, and came to share his grief. Keep the two verbs in mind. Job will soon call them miserable comforters (16:2). And at the very end, when his brothers and sisters come to eat with him, the narrator will say they showed him sympathy and comforted him (42:11), the same pair of words. The friends came to do something the book finally sees done by others.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And when they saw him from a distance, they did not recognize him. And they raised their voices and wept, and they tore their robes and sprinkled dust on their heads toward heaven.

They see a man on the ash heap and do not know him. The sores have changed his face. They weep aloud, tear their clothes as he tore his (1:20), and throw dust into the air so that it falls on their heads. It is real grief, and it is honest.

Isaiah's Servant is described the same way: his appearance was so marred, beyond human semblance (Isa 52:14). There is a kind of suffering that makes a man unrecognizable, and the Son of God went into it.

verseByVerse.quote: And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and no one spoke a word to him, for they saw that his suffering was very great.

Seven days was the time of mourning for the dead; Joseph mourned his father seven days (Gen 50:10). The friends mourn Job as though he were already dead. They sit on the ground with him, day and night, and say nothing, because they can see that nothing they could say would be big enough for his pain. They let him speak first.

This is the best thing the friends do in the whole book, and it is still the right place to begin with anyone in deep grief. Go. Sit on the ground. Do not explain. Weep with those who weep (Rom 12:15). When the friends open their mouths, from chapter 4 on, they will do great harm, and God will say at the end that they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Their silence never needed to be forgiven.

And this is what God did for us. He did not send an explanation from a distance. The Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14). He sat in our dust, and so we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses (Heb 4:15). He has been on the ground with us, and he stays.

3.title: Let the Day Perish
3.text: <sup>1</sup>After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth.<sup>2</sup>And Job said:<sup>3</sup>"Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.'<sup>4</sup>Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it.<sup>5</sup>Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.<sup>6</sup>That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months.<sup>7</sup>Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.<sup>8</sup>Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan.<sup>9</sup>Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning,<sup>10</sup>because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.<sup>11</sup>"Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire?<sup>12</sup>Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?<sup>13</sup>For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest,<sup>14</sup>with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves,<sup>15</sup>or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.<sup>16</sup>Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light?<sup>17</sup>There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest.<sup>18</sup>There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster.<sup>19</sup>The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.<sup>20</sup>"Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul,<sup>21</sup>who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,<sup>22</sup>who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?<sup>23</sup>Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?<sup>24</sup>For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water.<sup>25</sup>For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me.<sup>26</sup>I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
3.overview: After seven days of silence Job speaks, and curses the day of his birth. He wishes that day darkness and that night barren, struck from the calendar, cursed by those who rouse Leviathan, because it did not keep him from being born into trouble (vv. 1-10). He asks why he did not die at birth: then he would be at rest with kings and princes, or like a stillborn child, where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest (vv. 11-19). And he asks why light is given to the miserable who long for death, to a man whose way is hidden and whom God has hedged in; he has no ease, no quiet, no rest, but trouble comes (vv. 20-26).
3.theology:
Lament is not rebellion. Job curses his day, not his God, and Scripture places the same cry in the mouth of a faithful prophet (Jer 20:14-18) and lets whole psalms end in darkness (Ps 88). Christ himself prayed with loud cries and tears (Heb 5:7) and took the lament of Psalm 22 on his lips (Matt 27:46).

Job's let that day be darkness reverses God's let there be light (Gen 1:3). When God answers, he begins with creation (38:4). The longing for rest that Job seeks in the grave is answered in Christ (Matt 11:28).
3.examples:
Job curses the day, not God, and Satan's prediction fails again.

Let that day be darkness is let there be light run backwards.

The Leviathan Job wanted roused, God will show him on a lead (41:1).

He digs for the grave as for treasure; in chapter 28 men dig for treasure and cannot find wisdom.

He longs for death and leaves it in God's hands.

The rest-words of the grave come back with not in front of them.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After seven days Job speaks, and cursed the day of his birth (vv. 1-2): Let the day perish on which I was born (v. 3). He wishes it dark, claimed by gloom, struck from the calendar (vv. 4-6), its night barren, cursed by those who rouse Leviathan (vv. 7-8), its dawn never coming, because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb (vv. 9-10).
verseByVerse.theology: Satan said Job would curse God. He curses a day. Grief this deep is not the same thing as rebellion, and Scripture keeps the two apart.

verseByVerse.quote: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. And Job said:
verseByVerse.commentary:
After this Job opened his mouth and cursed the day of his birth. And Job said:

Seven days of silence end, and it is Job who breaks them. The friends have waited for him, as mourners should. And the first thing he does is curse. Not God, the day. Satan twice predicted that Job would curse God to his face (1:11; 2:5). He does not. He curses the day he was born, and the difference is the whole difference between a man in agony and a man in rebellion.

He is not the only servant of God to say it. Jeremiah, a faithful prophet in the middle of his calling, cried, Cursed be the day on which I was born! (Jer 20:14). Scripture does not tidy these cries away. It prints them, so that the believer who has felt the same thing will know he is not the first, and that God has heard it before.

Two things change here, and the reader should notice both. The book changes from prose to poetry: from And Job said until 42:6 almost everything is set out in lines, the way the Psalms are, and it is meant to be heard as the speech of a man in extremity, not as a statement of doctrine. And Job himself seems to change. The man who said blessed be the name of the LORD now wishes he had never been born. It is the same man. Seven days on the ash heap have passed, and the sores have not. When James holds Job up to Christians, the word he uses is steadfastness (James 5:11): not calm, but endurance, the refusal to let go while everything in you is shouting. This chapter is part of what James meant.

verseByVerse.quote: "Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, 'A man is conceived.' Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it. Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let the day perish on which I was born, and the night that said, A man is conceived. He goes back to the beginning, his birth and before that his conception, as if he could reach into the past and unmake it. The night is imagined speaking, announcing a boy. He wishes it had never spoken.

Let that day be darkness! May God above not seek it, nor light shine upon it. Anyone who knows Genesis will hear it. On the first day God said, Let there be light (Gen 1:3). Job uses the same Hebrew form in reverse: "let it be darkness". He wants to un-create his own day, to take it back into the dark before God spoke.

May God above not seek it. To seek a thing, in this sense, is to care for it. Moses told Israel that theirs was a land that the LORD your God cares for, with his eyes on it from the beginning of the year to the end of the year (Deut 11:12). Job asks God to take his eyes off one day, to stop caring for it, so that it falls out of existence. It is the prayer of a man who still believes that nothing lasts unless God keeps it.

Let gloom and deep darkness claim it. Let clouds dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. He piles up every word for dark he has. This is what grief does to a man's world: it runs back over his whole life and puts out the lights one by one.

One of those words matters for the rest of the book. Deep darkness is the Hebrew tsalmaveth, which older translations rendered "the shadow of death"; it is the word of the valley of the shadow of death (Ps 23:4). It runs all through Job. And the same man who here asks the deep darkness to swallow his day will say, a few chapters on, that God brings deep darkness to light (12:22), and God will ask him, have you seen the gates of deep darkness? (38:17). The darkness Job calls on is not beyond God's reach. He has seen its gates.

Keep Genesis in mind. When God finally answers Job, he will not start with Job's suffering. He will start with creation: Where were you when I laid the foundation of the earth? (38:4). Job has tried to undo a day. God will show him the One who made every day there is.

verseByVerse.quote: That night—let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months. Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
That night — let thick darkness seize it! Let it not rejoice among the days of the year; let it not come into the number of the months. Behold, let that night be barren; let no joyful cry enter it.

He wants the night struck off the calendar, so that it never comes round again. And he wants it barren. The joyful cry would have been the shout when a boy was born. Job wishes that there had been no one to shout for.

Hear what he is not saying. He is not saying his life was always misery; chapter 29 will show how rich it was. He is saying that if this is where it was heading, it would have been better never to have begun. Deep grief can do that to a person's past: it reaches back and poisons the happy years too. That is not a verdict on the years. It is a measure of the wound.

verseByVerse.quote: Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan. Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning, because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let those curse it who curse the day, who are ready to rouse up Leviathan. The ancient world believed in men who could curse a day and make it unlucky, and told stories of Leviathan, the monster of the sea and of chaos. Job reaches for any power at all that might undo his day, even the monster.

That name will come back. At the end of the book God will ask Job, Can you draw out Leviathan with a fishhook? (41:1), and will describe the creature Job wanted roused as something God made and holds on a lead. Scripture elsewhere uses the same name for every power that opposes God: In that day the LORD ... will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent (Isa 27:1). Job calls on chaos. God will show him that chaos has a master.

Let the stars of its dawn be dark; let it hope for light, but have none, nor see the eyelids of the morning, because it did not shut the doors of my mother's womb, nor hide trouble from my eyes. The eyelids of the morning is the first glimmer at dawn. He wants that night to wait for a morning that never comes, and he gives his reason: it let him be born, and so let him see trouble.

That word, 'amal, is the one Job keeps using for his life now: the misery of verse 20, the nights of misery of 7:3. And it is the word Eliphaz will seize on in his first reply: man is born to trouble as the sparks fly upward (5:7). Job says trouble came because he was born. Eliphaz will say trouble is what being born means, and that it does not come from nowhere. Listen for the word; the argument of the next twenty chapters is already starting.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–19 — Why Did I Not Die at Birth?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why did I not die at birth? (vv. 11-12). Then he would be at rest with kings and counselors and princes (vv. 13-15), or like a stillborn child who never saw the light (v. 16). There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest; the prisoner no longer hears the taskmaster, and the slave is free (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Job longs for the grave as a place of rest. The New Testament does not deny the longing. It points it to a person: Come to me ... and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did I not die at birth, come out from the womb and expire? Why did the knees receive me? Or why the breasts, that I should nurse?

Now the first why of the book, and there will be many. The knees are the mother's, or a father's, taking the newborn on his lap as his own; the breasts are the mother's feeding him. Every kindness that kept the baby alive, Job now counts as a cruelty. If they had let him die, he would not be here.

This is not the question of a philosopher. It is the question people ask in hospital corridors and at three in the morning. The Bible does not forbid it. Job asks it, and God will answer him, though not in the way he expects.

verseByVerse.quote: For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest, with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves, or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For then I would have lain down and been quiet; I would have slept; then I would have been at rest, with kings and counselors of the earth who rebuilt ruins for themselves, or with princes who had gold, who filled their houses with silver.

Quiet, sleep, rest. Those are the three things he cannot have, and in his pain the grave looks like the only place to find them. He pictures himself lying among the great: kings who built monuments, princes who hoarded gold. Rebuilt ruins for themselves may mean they restored ancient sites to make a name, or built palaces and tombs that are ruins now; either way, what they built for themselves did not keep them. They are all lying down now. Death has made them equal, and Job would rather be equal with the dead than go on living.

The Old Testament saints saw the grave dimly, as a place of silence and stillness, and Job speaks of it the way a desperate man does, as mere relief. The New Testament gives the longing its real answer. There is a rest for the weary, and it is not the grave; it is a person. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt 11:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light? There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest. There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Or why was I not as a hidden stillborn child, as infants who never see the light? The stillborn baby is buried quietly, unnamed; the light never touches it. Job envies it.

There the wicked cease from troubling, and there the weary are at rest. There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. The small and the great are there, and the slave is free from his master.

These lines have been carved on many gravestones, and they are true as far as they go. In the grave nobody bullies anyone. The taskmaster is the word Exodus uses for Egypt's slave drivers (Exod 3:7), and Job imagines the prisoners in the grave at last out of earshot of the shouting. The weak and the powerful, the slave and his owner, lie side by side. For a man in unending pain it sounds like freedom.

But Scripture's fuller word about the rest of the dead is for those who die in the Lord: Blessed indeed ... that they may rest from their labors (Rev 14:13). The rest Job longed for in the dark is real, and it belongs to those who belong to Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why is light given to him who is in misery? — to those who long for death and it does not come (vv. 20-22), to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in (v. 23). Sighs are his bread; what he feared has come; I have no rest, but trouble comes (vv. 24-26).
verseByVerse.theology: For the first time Job's question turns toward God. He does not doubt that God gives life. He cannot understand why God goes on giving it to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures, who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is light given to him who is in misery, and life to the bitter in soul, who long for death, but it comes not, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures, who rejoice exceedingly and are glad when they find the grave?

The question turns. It is no longer only about Job's birth; it is about everyone in misery, and it is aimed, carefully, at God. The Hebrew says simply "why does he give light", without naming him. Job still believes that God gives life. That is exactly his problem. If God gives life, why does he keep giving it to people who can only suffer?

Some who read this will know the longing from the inside, the wish to go to sleep and not wake. Look at what Job does with it. He says it aloud. He says it to God. And he never takes his life into his own hands; later he will ask God to end it (6:8-9), because he knows it is God's to give and God's to take (1:21). If that is where you are, do what Job did: say it aloud, to God and to someone who will sit with you on the ground.

And notice the picture of digging for death more than for hidden treasures. In chapter 28 men will dig into the earth for treasure, and Job will ask where wisdom, dearer than all of it, can be found (28:1-13). The man digging for the grave has not yet found what is buried deeper.

verseByVerse.quote: Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden, whom God has hedged in?

Now God is named. Whose way is hidden: Job cannot see where his road goes or why it turned. Hedged in: in the ESV it is the word Satan used in chapter 1, and the Hebrew words are close cousins. Satan complained that God had put a hedge around Job to protect him (1:10). Job feels the hedge as a prison wall. The same hand that once guarded him now seems to be shutting him in.

The reader knows what Job does not: that God is still guarding him, and that the limit set in heaven still stands (2:6). Every believer walks, some of the time, where his way is hidden. The hedge he feels as a prison may be the very thing that is keeping him.

verseByVerse.quote: For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water. For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me. I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
For my sighing comes instead of my bread, and my groanings are poured out like water. Sighing is his food; groaning runs out of him like water from a jar. The sores, the loss, the sleeplessness have taken over the ordinary things of life.

For the thing that I fear comes upon me, and what I dread befalls me. People sometimes take this to mean that Job's fears brought the disaster on him. The book says nothing of the kind; chapters 1 and 2 have told us exactly how this began. Job had always known how fragile his blessings were. He rose early to pray for his children (1:5). Now the thing he dreaded has happened, and it was not his dread that caused it.

I am not at ease, nor am I quiet; I have no rest, but trouble comes. Listen to the words. Ease, quiet, rest: they are the words he used of the grave (vv. 13, 17-18), now with not in front of each one. The dead have what he lacks. And the last word of his first speech is trouble.

The chapter ends there, in the dark, with no word of hope. Psalm 88 ends the same way: my companions have become darkness (Ps 88:18). Job's lament is not the sin Satan wanted; he has not cursed God. But it is not the whole truth either, and some of his later words God will call words without knowledge (38:2). Scripture lets a chapter end in darkness because that is where some of God's people have to sit for a while. And the Son of God sat there too. In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears (Heb 5:7), and on the cross he took a lament on his own lips: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Matt 27:46). God who said Let light shine out of darkness has shone into ours, in the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6).

4.title: Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?<sup>3</sup>Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands.<sup>4</sup>Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees.<sup>5</sup>But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.<sup>6</sup>Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?<sup>7</sup>"Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off?<sup>8</sup>As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same.<sup>9</sup>By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.<sup>10</sup>The roar of the lion, the voice of the fierce lion, the teeth of the young lions are broken.<sup>11</sup>The strong lion perishes for lack of prey, and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.<sup>12</sup>"Now a word was brought to me stealthily; my ear received the whisper of it.<sup>13</sup>Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men,<sup>14</sup>dread came upon me, and trembling, which made all my bones shake.<sup>15</sup>A spirit glided past my face; the hair of my flesh stood up.<sup>16</sup>It stood still, but I could not discern its appearance. A form was before my eyes; there was silence, then I heard a voice:<sup>17</sup>'Can mortal man be in the right before God? Can a man be pure before his Maker?<sup>18</sup>Even in his servants he puts no trust, and his angels he charges with error;<sup>19</sup>how much more those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust, who are crushed like the moth.<sup>20</sup>Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces; they perish forever without anyone regarding it.<sup>21</sup>Is not their tent-cord plucked up within them, do they not die, and that without wisdom?'
4.overview: Eliphaz, the first of the friends to speak, begins courteously: Job has strengthened the weak hands of others, but now that trouble has touched him he is dismayed; should not his fear of God be his confidence (vv. 1-6)? Then he states the friends' case: who that was innocent ever perished? Those who sow trouble reap it and perish by the blast of God's anger; even the strong lion dies and its cubs are scattered (vv. 7-11). He tells of a spirit that came to him stealthily in the night with a message: no mortal can be in the right before God; if God charges even his angels with error, men in houses of clay are crushed like the moth and die without wisdom (vv. 12-21).
4.theology:
The friends' case, stated here, is that suffering proves sin. God will say they did not speak rightly of him (42:7). Their error is a true rule (the wicked reap what they sow, Gal 6:7) read backwards from the harvest to the seed, which Jesus himself refused (Luke 13:2-5; John 9:2-3). The innocent do perish; the cross is the proof (Luke 23:47).

The vision's question, Can mortal man be in the right before God?, is the right one, and it is asked here to crush. The gospel answers it: God is just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus (Rom 3:26).
4.examples:
Eliphaz quotes Job's good works back to him as a rebuke.

He turns fear of God and integrity into a guarantee against loss.

The blast of God's anger is the Hebrew word for the wind that killed Job's children.

Five Hebrew words for lion in two verses.

A night vision with no face and no thus says the LORD.

A true question, asked to leave a man without hope.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — You Have Strengthened the Weak Hands
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz begins gently: If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? (vv. 1-2). Job has strengthened weak hands and feeble knees (vv. 3-4); now trouble has touched him, and he is dismayed (v. 5). Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope? (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The first friend to speak is the kindest, and the LORD will name him first when he says the friends did not speak rightly of him (42:7). A gentle voice can carry a false message.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: If one ventures a word with you, will you be impatient? Yet who can keep from speaking?

The debate begins, and it will run for twenty-four chapters. Before a word of it is read, the reader should know how it ends. When the LORD speaks at the close of the book, he will say to this man by name: My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). Everything Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar say must be read in that light. They will say many true things about God. They will be wrong about Job, and wrong about God's ways with him, and God will say so.

Eliphaz speaks first, probably as the eldest, and he is the most courteous. He asks permission, almost apologetically. But who can keep from speaking? The friends' seven days of silence were their best hour, and the man who could not keep quiet any longer is about to show why silence was better.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees. But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands. Your words have upheld him who was stumbling, and you have made firm the feeble knees.

A real tribute. Job had been the man others went to in trouble, and Eliphaz uses words Isaiah would later use of God's comfort to his people: Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees (Isa 35:3). Hebrews takes up the same words to rally tired Christians (Heb 12:12).

But now it has come to you, and you are impatient; it touches you, and you are dismayed. Here the tribute turns. You gave advice to others; now take it yourself. There is a hard truth in that, and every pastor knows it: it is easier to counsel suffering than to bear it. But Eliphaz has not stopped to measure what has come to Job. Ten children and his health are not the troubles Job used to talk other people through. The comforter who says "you of all people should cope with this" has not yet understood the size of the grief.

verseByVerse.quote: Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Is not your fear of God your confidence, and the integrity of your ways your hope?

These are the narrator's words from 1:1, and God's own from 1:8: fears God, integrity. Eliphaz does not deny Job's piety. He assumes it, and then turns it into a guarantee: if you really fear God, you have nothing to fear. A godly man cannot come to real harm.

That sounds like faith, and it has a true root: those who fear God are safe in him for ever. But Eliphaz means safe from loss, pain and grief in this life, and God never promised that. Job's fear of God is exactly the thing Satan attacked. It was his integrity that was on trial, not his insurance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — Who That Was Innocent Ever Perished?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz states the case the friends will hold to the end: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off? (v. 7). Those who sow trouble reap it, and perish by the blast of God's anger (vv. 8-9). Even the strong lion perishes, and its cubs are scattered (vv. 10-11).
verseByVerse.theology: It is a true rule about the end of the wicked, turned into a law about every sufferer. The cross breaks it: Certainly this man was innocent! (Luke 23:47).

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off? As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember: who that was innocent ever perished? Or where were the upright cut off?

Here is the friends' whole case in one sentence, and the rest of their speeches only repeat it: the innocent do not perish; therefore, if you are perishing, you are not innocent. It is put as a question, as though no one could possibly answer it.

Scripture answers it on almost every page. Abel was innocent and was killed in a field. Zechariah the priest was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD for speaking God's word (2 Chr 24:21). And one day a Roman officer would stand at the foot of a cross, watch a man die, and say, Certainly this man was innocent! (Luke 23:47). Where were the upright cut off? At Golgotha. Jesus refused Eliphaz's reasoning in so many words. Of the Galileans Pilate killed and the eighteen crushed by a tower: do you think that they were worse offenders than all the others ...? No, I tell you (Luke 13:4-5). Of a man born blind: It was not that this man sinned, or his parents (John 9:3).

As I have seen, those who plow iniquity and sow trouble reap the same. By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed. Paul says something that sounds the same: whatever one sows, that will he also reap (Gal 6:7). But Paul says it as a warning to the one doing the sowing. Eliphaz reads it backwards, from the harvest to the seed: you are reaping trouble, so you must have sown it. And note his words. Trouble is Job's own word from 3:10.
