Rahab here is a sea monster, not the woman of Jericho.

Without cause: Job says what God said in heaven.

If it is not he, who then is it? The reader knows.

Snow cannot wash Job clean; God washes whiter than snow.

No arbiter: 1 Timothy 2:5.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — How Can a Man Be in the Right Before God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job agrees: how can a man be in the right before God? No one could answer him once in a thousand (vv. 1-3). God moves mountains, shakes the earth, commands the sun, trampled the waves of the sea and made the stars (vv. 4-10). He passes by me, and I see him not; no one can ask him what he is doing; the helpers of Rahab bowed beneath him (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's hymn to God's power is as true as Eliphaz's. For Job it is not a comfort, because a God this great cannot be taken to court.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God? If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: Truly I know that it is so: But how can a man be in the right before God?

Job agrees with the friends' premise. This is the question Eliphaz's night visitor asked (4:17). But Job means something sharper. Be in the right is courtroom language: win your case. How could anyone take God to law and win?

If one wished to contend with him, one could not answer him once in a thousand times. God would ask a thousand questions and a man could not answer one. Job is more right than he knows. When God does speak, he will ask Job question after question (chs 38-41), and Job will say, I lay my hand on my mouth (40:4).

And the question is still the one every human being must face. How can a man be in the right with God? Job sees only a courtroom he cannot win. The gospel announces that the Judge himself has provided the righteousness (Rom 3:26).

verseByVerse.quote: He is wise in heart and mighty in strength— who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded?— he who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger, who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble; who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is wise in heart and mighty in strength — who has hardened himself against him, and succeeded? Pharaoh tried, and the sea closed over his army (Exod 14:17). No one fights God and wins.

He who removes mountains, and they know it not, when he overturns them in his anger, who shakes the earth out of its place, and its pillars tremble; who commands the sun, and it does not rise; who seals up the stars. Earthquakes, eclipses, stars hidden by storm: Job has watched the world shake, and he knows who shakes it. He does not doubt God's power for a moment. That is what makes his position so hard. A weak god could be excused. This one could stop Job's suffering with a word.

verseByVerse.quote: who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea; who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south; who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea; who made the Bear and Orion, the Pleiades and the chambers of the south; who does great things beyond searching out, and marvelous things beyond number.

Trampled the waves of the sea: God walks on the sea as a man walks on the ground. Keep that picture; it will come back in a moment. The constellations he names are the ones God will name when he answers: Can you bind the chains of the Pleiades or loose the cords of Orion? (38:31). Amos praised the same Maker (Amos 5:8).

The last line is Eliphaz's, almost word for word (5:9). Job and the friends agree about God's greatness. They do not disagree about who God is. They disagree about what his greatness means for a man in pain. For the friends it proves that everything is in order. For Job it means there is no one above God to appeal to.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him. Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, 'What are you doing?' "God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, he passes by me, and I see him not; he moves on, but I do not perceive him.

God is at work all around him, and Job cannot see him. He feels the effects and never the presence. Many believers in the dark have said exactly this.

Now put two verses together. God trampled the waves of the sea (v. 8), and he passes by me, and I see him not (v. 11). On a night on the Sea of Galilee, with the disciples rowing hard against the wind, Jesus came to them, walking on the sea. He meant to pass by them (Mark 6:48). They saw him, took him for a ghost, and were terrified. But immediately he spoke to them and said, Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Mark 6:50). The God who walks the waves and passes by unseen in Job's complaint walked the waves in a body, and passed by, and was seen, and spoke. Job longed for God to come near in a form he could meet. In Christ he did.

Behold, he snatches away; who can turn him back? Who will say to him, What are you doing? Nebuchadnezzar learned the same: none can stay his hand or say to him, What have you done? (Dan 4:35). God will not turn back his anger; beneath him bowed the helpers of Rahab. This Rahab is not the woman of Jericho. It is the name of a sea monster, a picture of chaos and of every power that sets itself against God: was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces? (Isa 51:9). If the monsters of chaos bow to him, what hope has Job of standing up to him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–24 — If It Is a Matter of Justice, Who Can Summon Him?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How can Job answer him? Though in the right, he must plead for mercy (vv. 14-16). God crushes him with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause (vv. 17-18). If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him? (v. 19). I am blameless (vv. 20-21). He destroys both the blameless and the wicked; if it is not he, who then is it? (vv. 22-24).
verseByVerse.theology: Job is right that his wounds are without cause, and says so in God's own word. He is wrong, and says too much, when he claims that God mocks the innocent.

verseByVerse.quote: How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser. If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
How then can I answer him, choosing my words with him? Though I am in the right, I cannot answer him; I must appeal for mercy to my accuser.

A man who is innocent would normally demand justice. Job says: before God, even an innocent man could only beg for mercy. The one he would have to plead with is the one he feels is prosecuting him.

If I summoned him and he answered me, I would not believe that he was listening to my voice. This is the despair of unanswered prayer: even if God answered, I would not believe he had heard. And yet Job keeps summoning him. He does not stop talking to God because he doubts God listens. That is faith of a kind the friends never show.

verseByVerse.quote: For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause; he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness. If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him?
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he crushes me with a tempest and multiplies my wounds without cause; he will not let me get my breath, but fills me with bitterness.

Without cause. It is the word Satan used, does Job fear God for no reason? (1:9), and the word God used, you incited me against him to destroy him without reason (2:3). Job has no idea those words were spoken. He says exactly what God said. His wounds really are without cause in him. On that point Job is right and the friends are wrong.

And the tempest that crushes him is, in Hebrew, a word that sounds the same as the whirlwind out of which the LORD will finally answer him (38:1). The storm he complains of is the storm God will speak from.

If it is a contest of strength, behold, he is mighty! If it is a matter of justice, who can summon him? No court can issue God a summons. That is Job's dilemma in one line.

From this chapter on, the reader needs to hear Job's speeches as a lawsuit. He uses the words of a court: contend, answer, summon, in the right, arbiter. He is not asking for his health back so much as for a hearing, a verdict that he is innocent. He will say, I have prepared my case (13:18), I would lay my case before him (23:4), and at last he will sign his defence like a legal document: Here is my signature! Let the Almighty answer me! (31:35). The book's climax is that God does answer. Not with a verdict on the charges, but with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse. I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me; though I am blameless, he would prove me perverse. I am blameless; I regard not myself; I loathe my life.

I am blameless: God's own word for him (1:1, 8; 2:3), and Job says it of himself. He is not boasting. He is refusing to confess what is not true, even though a false confession might end the argument. But he is afraid that under God's cross-examination he would be tripped up and made to look guilty. I regard not myself: he no longer cares what happens to him. That is the exhaustion of a man who has lost the will to protect himself.

verseByVerse.quote: It is all one; therefore I say, 'He destroys both the blameless and the wicked.' When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges— if it is not he, who then is it?
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is all one; therefore I say, He destroys both the blameless and the wicked. When disaster brings sudden death, he mocks at the calamity of the innocent. The earth is given into the hand of the wicked; he covers the faces of its judges — if it is not he, who then is it?

Here Job says too much, and the reader must see it. That the same disasters fall on good and bad alike is true; the Preacher says so (Eccl 9:2). But that God mocks the innocent in their calamity is not true, and God will call such talk words without knowledge (38:2) and ask Job, Will you condemn me that you may be in the right? (40:8). A sufferer may say this in the dark. He must not build a theology on it.

And look at Job's last question: if it is not he, who then is it? The reader can answer it. It was the accuser (1:12; 2:7), acting under God's permission and within God's limit. Job sees only two possibilities, that God is doing this or no one is. The prologue shows a third that he cannot see. God rules over it all, and God does not mock.

Even his complaint that the earth is given into the hand of the wicked is truer than he knows. In the council God said to Satan, all that he has is in your hand (1:12). John says the same of the world as a whole: the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). But the hand that gave it can take it back, and the same letter says, The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil (1 John 3:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–35 — There Is No Arbiter Between Us
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His days flee away (vv. 25-26). He cannot put on a cheerful face (vv. 27-29). Though he washed with snow, God would plunge him in the pit (vv. 30-31). For he is not a man, as I am. There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both (vv. 32-33). If God would take away his rod, Job could speak without fear (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: Job describes exactly the one he needs: someone who is God's equal and his, who could put a hand on each. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good. They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey. If I say, 'I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer,' I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My days are swifter than a runner; they flee away; they see no good. They go by like skiffs of reed, like an eagle swooping on the prey. A royal runner, a light papyrus boat racing downstream, an eagle diving: three pictures of speed, on land, on water, in the air. His life is rushing past and all of it is bad.

If I say, I will forget my complaint, I will put off my sad face, and be of good cheer, I become afraid of all my suffering, for I know you will not hold me innocent. Every sufferer has been told to cheer up. Job has tried. He resolves to put on a brighter face, and the fear comes back, because nothing has changed. Forced cheerfulness is no cure for grief, and the church should never demand it.

verseByVerse.quote: I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain? If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I shall be condemned; why then do I labor in vain? If I wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, yet you will plunge me into a pit, and my own clothes will abhor me.

Snow water, the cleanest there is; lye, the strongest soap. Scrub as he may, God would push him back into the filth, and his very clothes would be disgusted to wear him. Job means: whatever I do, the verdict is fixed.

He has stumbled on a truth bigger than his case. No one can wash himself clean before God. Though you wash yourself with lye and use much soap, the stain of your guilt is still before me (Jer 2:22). But the same God who says so offers the washing himself: Come now, let us reason together, says the LORD: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow (Isa 1:18). David prayed for it: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow (Ps 51:7). The snow Job cannot wash with, God washes with.

verseByVerse.quote: For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together. There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him, that we should come to trial together. There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.

This is the heart of the chapter and one of the great moments of the book. Job's problem is not only that God is strong. It is that God is not a man. There is no common ground on which they could meet as equals. What he needs is an arbiter, a mediator who could stand between them and lay one hand on God and one on Job, belonging to both, trusted by both.

The word arbiter comes from the verb God uses in Isaiah 1:18, let us reason together. Job thinks a hearing is impossible. God himself proposes one, and ends it with snow-white cleansing.

And Job has described, without knowing it, the one God would send. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim 2:5). The man: God, who is not a man as Job is, became one, so that the hand that holds God's throne could also be laid on us. Job cries that there is no arbiter. Every Christian can answer him by name. And this is only the first step. Job will reach higher: to a witness in heaven (16:19), and to a Redeemer who lives (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me. Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him take his rod away from me, and let not dread of him terrify me. Then I would speak without fear of him, for I am not so in myself.

If only the beating would stop and the terror lift, Job could speak his case calmly. He does not think himself guilty; it is the dread that silences him.

The gospel does what Job asks. The rod was not simply taken away; it was laid on another: upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace (Isa 53:5). And so the Christian can do what Job could not, and speak to God without dread: Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace (Heb 4:16). Perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18).

10.title: Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
10.text: <sup>1</sup>"I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul.<sup>2</sup>I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.<sup>3</sup>Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?<sup>4</sup>Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees?<sup>5</sup>Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years,<sup>6</sup>that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin,<sup>7</sup>although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?<sup>8</sup>Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether.<sup>9</sup>Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?<sup>10</sup>Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese?<sup>11</sup>You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.<sup>12</sup>You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.<sup>13</sup>Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose.<sup>14</sup>If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity.<sup>15</sup>If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.<sup>16</sup>And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me.<sup>17</sup>You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.<sup>18</sup>"Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me<sup>19</sup>and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.<sup>20</sup>Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer<sup>21</sup>before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow,<sup>22</sup>the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
10.overview: Job speaks to God in the bitterness of his soul: do not condemn me; tell me why you contend with me. Does it please God to despise the work of his hands? Has he eyes of flesh, or a man's short days, that he must search out Job's sin, though he knows Job is not guilty (vv. 1-7)? God's hands made him like clay, poured him out like milk, knit him with bones and sinews, and granted him life and steadfast love; yet this was hidden in God's heart. Guilty or innocent, Job cannot lift his head; God hunts him like a lion and brings fresh troops against him (vv. 8-17). Why did God bring him out of the womb? Let God leave him alone a little before he goes to the land of darkness and deep shadow (vv. 18-22).
10.theology:
Job never learns the reason for his suffering, and the book shows it is possible to rest in God without it. God does not despise the work of his hands; he completes it (Phil 1:6). The purpose hidden in God's heart (v. 13) was delight in Job (1:8), and the care Job feels as scrutiny (7:18) has preserved his spirit (v. 12).

The God who knit Job with skin and sinews in the womb promises to do it again at the resurrection (Ezek 37:6). The land of deep darkness has seen a great light (Isa 9:2; Matt 4:16).
10.examples:
Let me know why: Job is never told.

Although you know that I am not guilty: God does know.

Milk, cheese, skin, flesh, bones and sinews: the womb; Ezekiel 37: the resurrection.

Your care and visit him every morning are one Hebrew root.

God's hidden purpose was real, and it was delight.

The land of deep darkness and Isaiah 9:2.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Let Me Know Why You Contend Against Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me (vv. 1-2). Does it please God to despise the work of his hands (v. 3)? Has he eyes of flesh, or days like a man's, that he must search out Job's sin, although you know that I am not guilty (vv. 4-7)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks for the one thing he will never be given: the reason. God knows he is not guilty, just as Job says.

verseByVerse.quote: "I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I loathe my life; I will give free utterance to my complaint; I will speak in the bitterness of my soul. I will say to God, Do not condemn me; let me know why you contend against me.

Job goes on straight from chapter 9, still speaking to God. He asks two things. Do not condemn me: I am not guilty. And tell me the charge. What is the case against me? Why are you fighting me? He will ask for it again at the end: Oh, that I had the indictment written by my adversary! (31:35).

Here is something the reader should notice now, because it matters for anyone who suffers. Job never gets his answer. Not in this chapter, not when God speaks from the whirlwind, not in the happy ending. He is never told about the council in heaven. The reader is told, and Job is not. He has to come to rest in God himself without ever learning why. Most believers in deep suffering will live and die in the same place. The book shows that it is possible to be at peace there.

verseByVerse.quote: Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does it seem good to you to oppress, to despise the work of your hands and favor the designs of the wicked?

A craftsman does not smash his own best work. Why would God? Job is appealing to God's own character, and he is right to. The psalmist prays in the same way: Do not forsake the work of your hands (Ps 138:8). Isaiah: we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand (Isa 64:8).

And the New Testament gives the answer Job reaches for: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ (Phil 1:6). God does not despise the work of his hands. He finishes it.

verseByVerse.quote: Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees? Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years, that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin, although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Have you eyes of flesh? Do you see as man sees? Are your days as the days of man, or your years as a man's years, that you seek out my iniquity and search for my sin, although you know that I am not guilty, and there is none to deliver out of your hand?

A human investigator has limited sight and limited time, so he presses a suspect hard to get at the truth before it is too late. But God does not see as man sees (1 Sam 16:7); he looks on the heart. He has all eternity. Why, then, treat Job like a suspect under interrogation?

Although you know that I am not guilty. The reader knows this is exactly true. God said it himself, twice (1:8; 2:3). Job is not being proud. He is saying what God has already said. His mistake is only in thinking that God's hand on him means God doubts him.

There is none to deliver out of your hand is a line from the song of Moses: I wound and I heal; and there is none that can deliver out of my hand (Deut 32:39). Eliphaz quoted the first half, that God wounds and heals (5:18). Job quotes the second: no one can get me out of your hand. The same hand that holds him is the only hand that could heal him, and Job knows it. He has nowhere else to go.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–17 — Your Hands Fashioned and Made Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether (v. 8). God made him like clay, formed him in the womb, knit him with bones and sinews (vv. 9-11), and granted me life and steadfast love (v. 12). Yet these things you hid in your heart (v. 13). Guilty or innocent, he cannot lift his head; God hunts him like a lion and brings fresh troops against him (vv. 14-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Job remembers God's tenderness and cannot square it with his suffering. The chapter's answer is in his own words: the care that preserved his spirit has not stopped.

verseByVerse.quote: Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether. Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Your hands fashioned and made me, and now you have destroyed me altogether. Remember that you have made me like clay; and will you return me to the dust?

Job remembers where he came from. God formed man of dust from the ground (Gen 2:7), and said that to dust he would return (Gen 3:19). Job asks: after taking such care to make me, will you simply grind me back into the dust? It is a plea from the potter's own workmanship. You made me. Remember that.

verseByVerse.quote: Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews. You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews.

This is the ancient world's picture of a child forming in the womb: something liquid set into shape, like milk thickening into cheese, then clothed in skin and flesh, then bound together with bone and sinew. The psalmist sings the same wonder: you knitted me together in my mother's womb (Ps 139:13). Job knows he is not an accident. God made him, carefully, from the inside.

And there is a hope hidden in that list which Job cannot yet see. Ezekiel, looking at a valley of dry bones, heard God promise, I will lay sinews upon you, and will cause flesh to come upon you, and cover you with skin, and put breath in you, and you shall live (Ezek 37:6). The same materials, gathered again. The God who knit Job together in the womb can knit him together again from the grave.

You have granted me life and steadfast love, and your care has preserved my spirit. Here, in the middle of his complaint, is the loveliest line in the chapter. Steadfast love is chesed, God's covenant loyalty. And your care comes from the same Hebrew root as the complaint of 7:18, that God would visit him every morning and test him. The visiting that Job felt as surveillance is, in his own better words, the care that has kept his spirit alive. He has the answer in his mouth and cannot yet see it.

verseByVerse.quote: Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose. If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity. If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Yet these things you hid in your heart; I know that this was your purpose.

Job suspects that God's kindness was a trap: that all along, behind the care, God was planning this. And he is half right. God did have a purpose hidden from him, settled in heaven before a single blow fell. But the purpose was not malice. It began with God saying, Have you considered my servant Job? (1:8). What God hid in his heart was delight in Job, and a purpose to show the world a man who would trust him for no reason. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28). A believer may be sure of that hidden purpose even when, like Job, he never sees it.

If I sin, you watch me and do not acquit me of my iniquity. If I am guilty, woe to me! If I am in the right, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with disgrace and look on my affliction. Trapped either way: guilty, and he is lost; innocent, and he still sits in shame. But Scripture has a name for God that answers this line: you, O LORD, are ... the lifter of my head (Ps 3:3).

verseByVerse.quote: And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me. You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And were my head lifted up, you would hunt me like a lion and again work wonders against me. You renew your witnesses against me and increase your vexation toward me; you bring fresh troops against me.

If he tried to stand, God would stalk him like a lion. The witnesses are his own wasted body, which seems to testify against him (16:8): everyone who sees his sores assumes his guilt. And the attacks come in waves, one fresh regiment after another. Job describes God as a hunter, a prosecutor and a general all at once. It is how things look from the ash heap. It is not how they are.

Notice work wonders against me. Eliphaz praised God who does marvelous things without number (5:9), and Job agreed (9:10). Now the wonders seem to be turned on him. The same power that fills the psalms with praise feels, from inside the pain, like an ambush. It is the same God, and the same power; what Job cannot yet see is its direction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Why did you bring me out from the womb? (vv. 18-19). His days are few; let God leave him alone a little before he goes to the land of darkness and deep shadow, where light itself is darkness (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The land Job dreads is the one Isaiah said would see a great light, and Matthew says the light dawned when Jesus came.

verseByVerse.quote: "Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Why did you bring me out from the womb? Would that I had died before any eye had seen me and were as though I had not been, carried from the womb to the grave.

He returns to the wish of chapter 3, but with a difference that matters. In chapter 3 he cursed his day and asked the dark to swallow it. Now he says you: why did you bring me out? The question is the same; it has become a prayer. That is movement. Job is still in the dark, but he is now talking to God in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer before I go—and I shall not return— to the land of darkness and deep shadow, the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are not my days few? Then cease, and leave me alone, that I may find a little cheer before I go — and I shall not return — to the land of darkness and deep shadow, the land of gloom like thick darkness, like deep shadow without any order, where light is as thick darkness.

A little cheer is the word of 9:27, the brighter face he could not put on. He asks only for a short breathing space before he dies. Then he describes the grave: darkness piled on darkness, without any order, a place where even the light is dark. It is creation undone, the world before God said Let there be light, the dark Job wished on his birthday (3:4-5).

But hear what the prophets say about that land. The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone (Isa 9:2). Deep darkness is Job's word, tsalmaveth. And Matthew says the light dawned when Jesus began to preach in Galilee: for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned (Matt 4:16). The land Job dreads has been visited. Christ abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel (2 Tim 1:10).

11.title: Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
11.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right?<sup>3</sup>Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?<sup>4</sup>For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'<sup>5</sup>But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you,<sup>6</sup>and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.<sup>7</sup>"Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty?<sup>8</sup>It is higher than heaven —what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know?<sup>9</sup>Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.<sup>10</sup>If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back?<sup>11</sup>For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it?<sup>12</sup>But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!<sup>13</sup>"If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him.<sup>14</sup>If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents.<sup>15</sup>Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.<sup>16</sup>You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away.<sup>17</sup>And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.<sup>18</sup>And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security.<sup>19</sup>You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.<sup>20</sup>But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
11.overview: Zophar will not let Job's many words go unanswered. Job claims his doctrine is pure and he is clean in God's eyes; if only God would speak and show him the secrets of wisdom, for God exacts of him less than his guilt deserves (vv. 1-6). The deep things of God are higher than heaven and deeper than Sheol; God summons the court and no one can stop him; he sees iniquity; a stupid man will understand when a wild donkey's colt is born a man (vv. 7-12). If Job will pray and put away iniquity, he will lift up his face, forget his misery, and his darkness will be like the morning; he will have hope and rest, and many will court his favour. But the hope of the wicked is to breathe their last (vv. 13-20).
11.theology:
That God punishes us less than our sins deserve (Ezra 9:13; Ps 103:10) is a truth for confession, not a verdict to pass on a sufferer; God had said Job suffered without reason (2:3), and judged Zophar's speech (42:7-9).

God's depth and height are beyond finding out (vv. 7-9). Zophar uses them to silence Job; Paul uses the same four dimensions for the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Eph 3:18-19).
11.examples:
Clean in God's eyes: mocked by Zophar, said by God.

Oh, that God would speak: he will, and against Zophar.

Less than your guilt deserves: a truth to say of yourself, never of another.

The four dimensions of God's wisdom, and of Christ's love.

Job's wild donkey turned into an insult.

Many will court your favor: the three friends, at 42:8-9.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — God Exacts of You Less Than Your Guilt Deserves
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zophar will not let Job's multitude of words go unanswered (vv. 1-3). Job claims to be pure; if only God would speak to him and show him the secrets of wisdom (vv. 4-6)! Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The third friend goes further than the other two: Job is getting off lightly. God, who called Job's suffering without reason (2:3), will say Zophar did not speak rightly (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: "Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right? Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said: Should a multitude of words go unanswered, and a man full of talk be judged right? Should your babble silence men, and when you mock, shall no one shame you?

The third friend is the bluntest. Eliphaz appealed to a vision and Bildad to the fathers; Zophar appeals to nothing but his own certainty. The case the friends share was set out in chapter 4, and Zophar repeats it. What he adds is harsher: Job deserves worse than he is getting. And Zophar is named with the others when God sends them to Job for his prayers (42:9).

He hears Job's two long speeches as babble, a flood of words, and Job's questions to God as mockery. That is how lament often sounds to people who have not suffered: too long, too loud, irreverent. But the man who has lost ten children has not said too much. He has said what he feels, to God, and God will take his words more seriously than Zophar does.

verseByVerse.quote: For you say, 'My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
For you say, My doctrine is pure, and I am clean in God's eyes.

Zophar summarises Job, and not fairly. Job never claimed his doctrine was pure; he has been pleading with God, not lecturing on theology. He claimed to be innocent of anything that could explain this (9:21; 10:7). And here is the irony again: clean in God's eyes is exactly what God said of him, a blameless and upright man (1:8). Zophar mocks as arrogance the verdict heaven has already given.

verseByVerse.quote: But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you, and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding. Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But oh, that God would speak and open his lips to you, and that he would tell you the secrets of wisdom! For he is manifold in understanding.

Zophar wishes God would speak. He is sure God would take his side. His wish will be granted: the LORD will speak (38:1), and when he has finished speaking to Job, he will turn to the friends and say, you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7).

Know then that God exacts of you less than your guilt deserves. This is Zophar's hardest line. Your suffering is real, says Zophar, but you have earned more. It is true of every sinner before God. Ezra confessed, you, our God, have punished us less than our iniquities deserved (Ezra 9:13), and the psalmist, He does not deal with us according to our sins (Ps 103:10). A believer may say that about himself on his knees, and he should. No one may say it about another person in pain. God had already said that Job's suffering was without reason (2:3). Zophar has taken a truth for confession and made it a weapon.

The secrets of wisdom Zophar wished God would tell were told in the end, and they were not what he expected. We impart a secret and hidden wisdom of God, which God decreed before the ages for our glory (1 Cor 2:7), and Paul's secret wisdom is Christ crucified, the innocent one who suffered for the guilty.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — Can You Find Out the Deep Things of God?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Can you find out the deep things of God? They are higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth, broader than the sea (vv. 7-9). If God passes through and summons the court, who can stop him? He knows worthless men (vv. 10-11). A stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: True words about God's greatness, used to shut a sufferer's mouth. Paul uses the same four dimensions for the love of Christ (Eph 3:18-19).

verseByVerse.quote: "Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven —what can you do? Deeper than Sheol—what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Can you find out the deep things of God? Can you find out the limit of the Almighty? It is higher than heaven — what can you do? Deeper than Sheol — what can you know? Its measure is longer than the earth and broader than the sea.

Up to the sky, down to the grave, out to the ends of the earth and across the sea: God's wisdom fills every direction, and no man can measure it. This is true, and fine, and Zophar means it as a gag: you cannot understand God, so stop arguing with him. He does not notice that it applies to him too. If God's ways cannot be found out, Zophar cannot find out why Job is suffering.

Paul uses the same four dimensions, and uses them the other way. He prays that Christians may have strength to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge (Eph 3:18-19). God's depth is not a wall to keep sufferers quiet. It is the size of the love that holds them.

verseByVerse.quote: If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back? For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it? But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man!
verseByVerse.commentary:
If he passes through and imprisons and summons the court, who can turn him back? Job said these very things: he passes by me and who can turn him back? (9:11-12). Zophar hands Job's words back to him. You admit God can do as he pleases; then accept his verdict.

For he knows worthless men; when he sees iniquity, will he not consider it? God sees what men hide. True; and the one thing God has seen in Job is integrity (2:3).

But a stupid man will get understanding when a wild donkey's colt is born a man! A proverb for the impossible. Job had compared his cry to a wild donkey's bray (6:5). Zophar takes the image and throws it back as an insult: you have as much chance of understanding as a donkey has of giving birth to a human being. When God speaks, he will talk about the wild donkey too, with pleasure, as a creature he set free (39:5). God is gentler with donkeys than Zophar is with his friend.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–20 — If You Prepare Your Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If Job will stretch out his hands to God and put away his iniquity, he will lift up his face, forget his misery, and his darkness will be like the morning (vv. 13-17). He will have hope and rest, and many will court his favour (vv. 18-19). But the eyes of the wicked will fail ... their hope is to breathe their last (v. 20).
verseByVerse.theology: Zophar's promises will largely come true, and the three friends will be among those who come seeking Job's favour (42:8-9).

verseByVerse.quote: "If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents. Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If you prepare your heart, you will stretch out your hands toward him. If iniquity is in your hand, put it far away, and let not injustice dwell in your tents.

Hands stretched out toward God is the posture of prayer. Zophar's advice is good advice for anyone who has sinned: set your heart right, pray, put away what is wrong. But it assumes the thing in question. Job's hands are not full of iniquity; he has said he would wash them in snow if it would do any good (9:30).

Surely then you will lift up your face without blemish; you will be secure and will not fear. Without blemish is the word used for an animal fit for sacrifice. Zophar promises that Job will be able to look God in the face again. He will, in the end, and it will not be because he confessed Zophar's list.

verseByVerse.quote: You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away. And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning. And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security. You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You will forget your misery; you will remember it as waters that have passed away. And your life will be brighter than the noonday; its darkness will be like the morning.

The misery will be like a flash flood that roared through the wadi and is gone. And Zophar reverses Job's own words. Job described the grave as the place where light is as thick darkness (10:22). Zophar says: repent, and your darkness will be like the morning. For those who belong to God it is even truer than he knew: night will be no more ... for the Lord God will be their light (Rev 22:5).

And you will feel secure, because there is hope; you will look around and take your rest in security. You will lie down, and none will make you afraid; many will court your favor. Hope, the thing Job said his days had run out of (7:6); rest, the thing he said he could not find (3:26). Many will court your favor: people will come to ask for his help. Read the last chapter. The first to come asking for Job's favour will be Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, with seven bulls and seven rams, needing his prayers (42:8-9).

You will lie down, and none will make you afraid is the covenant blessing of Leviticus word for word: you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid (Lev 26:6). Eliphaz reached for Deuteronomy's curses to describe the wicked (5:14); Zophar reaches for Leviticus' blessings to describe the repentant. Both treat Job's life as a ledger in which every entry can be read off his circumstances. The blessings are real, and Micah sees them at last for all God's people, every man under his vine and under his fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid (Mic 4:4). But they are gifts of grace, not a receipt for a confession.

verseByVerse.quote: But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last."
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the eyes of the wicked will fail; all way of escape will be lost to them, and their hope is to breathe their last.

The sting in the tail. The wicked will have only one hope left: to die. Zophar has chosen his words. Job said, Oh that I might have my request, and that God would fulfill my hope, that it would please God to crush me (6:8-9). Zophar now says that a man whose only hope is death is a wicked man. He has taken a sufferer's cry of despair and entered it as evidence against him.

That is a warning to every comforter. The things a person says in the worst hour are not a confession to be used against him. They are a cry to be answered. God answered Job's, and he answers ours in Christ, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light (2 Tim 1:10).

12.title: With God Are Wisdom and Might
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you.<sup>3</sup>But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?<sup>4</sup>I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock.<sup>5</sup>In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip.<sup>6</sup>The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.<sup>7</sup>"But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you;<sup>8</sup>or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you.<sup>9</sup>Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?<sup>10</sup>In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.<sup>11</sup>Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food?<sup>12</sup>Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.<sup>13</sup>"With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding.<sup>14</sup>If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open.<sup>15</sup>If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land.<sup>16</sup>With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.<sup>17</sup>He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools.<sup>18</sup>He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips.<sup>19</sup>He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty.<sup>20</sup>He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders.<sup>21</sup>He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.<sup>22</sup>He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light.<sup>23</sup>He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away.<sup>24</sup>He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste.<sup>25</sup>They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
12.overview: Job answers with sarcasm: wisdom will die with the friends; but he knows all they know. He, a just and blameless man who called to God and was answered, is a laughingstock; the comfortable despise the man who slips, while robbers are at peace (vv. 1-6). Ask the beasts, birds, bushes and fish: they know that the hand of the LORD has done this; in his hand is every life and breath. The ear tests words; wisdom is said to be with the aged (vv. 7-12). But with God are wisdom and might. What he tears down none rebuilds; the deceived and the deceiver are his; he strips counselors, judges, kings, priests and elders, brings deep darkness to light, raises and destroys nations, and makes their leaders grope in the dark (vv. 13-25).
12.theology:
Wisdom and might belong to God, not to the aged or the learned (v. 13); he overturns every human wisdom that thinks it has him measured (1 Cor 1:19-20). The only use of the covenant name in the debate is Job's confession that the hand of the LORD has done this (v. 9; Isa 41:20).

God brings deep darkness to light (v. 22); therefore no one should pronounce judgment before the time (1 Cor 4:5). Christ holds the keys that no one can overrule (v. 14; Rev 3:7).
12.examples:
Wisdom will die with you: Job's sarcasm.

The comfortable despise the man who slips.

The only LORD in chapters 3-37 is at verse 9.

Elihu quotes verse 11 almost word for word.

If he shuts a man in, none can open: the key of David, Revelation 3:7.

Psalm 107:40 joins verses 21 and 24.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Wisdom Will Die with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you (vv. 1-2). Job knows as much as they do (v. 3). He, a just and blameless man, has become a laughingstock (v. 4); the comfortable despise the man who slips (v. 5), while robbers live at peace (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's first answer to the friends' wisdom is to notice what it has made of him: a joke.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you. But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: No doubt you are the people, and wisdom will die with you. But I have understanding as well as you; I am not inferior to you. Who does not know such things as these?

Job has had three speeches from three friends, and he answers with sarcasm. You are the people who matter; when you die, wisdom dies with you. Then he says it plainly: I know everything you have said. God is great, the wicked perish, no one is pure before him: who does not know such things? The friends have been telling Job what he taught others for years (4:3-4). Their theology is not wrong because it is new. It is wrong because it is being used on the wrong man.

This speech closes the first round of the debate, and it is Job's longest yet, running to the end of chapter 14. Here he takes the friends' own subject, God's wisdom and power, and shows that it cuts against them.

verseByVerse.quote: I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock. In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip. The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am a laughingstock to my friends; I, who called to God and he answered me, a just and blameless man, am a laughingstock. The man who prayed and was answered, whom God himself called blameless (1:1), is now a joke to the men who came to comfort him.

In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip. A sharp piece of observation. Comfortable people find it easy to despise the unfortunate; contempt is always waiting for the man who stumbles. The psalmist knew it: Our soul has had more than enough of the scorn of those who are at ease (Ps 123:4). The friends are at ease. Their homes are standing, their children alive. It is easy, from there, to explain why someone else's fell.

The tents of robbers are at peace, and those who provoke God are secure, who bring their god in their hand. And look at the facts, says Job: plenty of wicked men are doing very well. Their god is in their hand, their own strength, as the prophet said of Babylon, whose own might is their god (Hab 1:11). Asaph nearly lost his faith over the same sight: I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked (Ps 73:3). If suffering proves guilt, prosperity should prove innocence, and it plainly does not.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ask the beasts, the birds, the bushes and the fish: who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? (vv. 7-9). In his hand is the life of every living thing (v. 10). The ear tests words as the palate tastes food; wisdom is said to be with the aged (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: The only time in the whole debate that anyone uses the covenant name of God, and it is Job, saying that everything is in the LORD's hand.

verseByVerse.quote: "But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you; or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you. Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this? In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But ask the beasts, and they will teach you; the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you; or the bushes of the earth, and they will teach you; and the fish of the sea will declare to you. Who among all these does not know that the hand of the LORD has done this?

You say you have wisdom. Every animal in the field knows as much. Creation itself testifies that everything that happens comes from God's hand. That is not a secret the friends discovered.

And notice the name. The LORD, God's covenant name, appears nowhere else in the whole debate from chapter 3 to chapter 37. Everyone, Job included, says God or the Almighty. Here, once, Job's deepest conviction breaks through in the name God gave his people, and the words are exactly those of Isaiah: that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it (Isa 41:20). Job does not believe his suffering came from chance or from men. It came through the LORD's hand. That is his agony, and it is also the ground under his feet.

In his hand is the life of every living thing and the breath of all mankind. Paul said it to the philosophers of Athens: God gives to all mankind life and breath and everything (Acts 17:25). Every breath Job draws on the ash heap is given to him by the God he is arguing with.

verseByVerse.quote: Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food? Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Does not the ear test words as the palate tastes food? Job said something like it before (6:30). The ear can tell good words from bad, as the tongue can tell good food from spoiled. Test what you are being told. Elihu will later quote this line almost word for word (34:3).

Wisdom is with the aged, and understanding in length of days. Taken alone it sounds like a proverb Job agrees with. But the next line answers it: With God are wisdom and might (v. 13). Job is probably repeating the friends' claim, the grey-haired men's confidence in their years, in order to set it beside the real source. Elihu, the youngest man present, will say it outright: It is not the old who are wise (32:9).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–25 — With God Are Wisdom and Might
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: With God are wisdom and might (v. 13). What he tears down no one rebuilds; he withholds and sends the waters; the deceived and the deceiver are his (vv. 14-16). He strips counselors, judges, kings, priests and elders (vv. 17-21), brings deep darkness to light, raises and destroys nations, and leaves their leaders groping in the dark (vv. 22-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's God overturns the wise and the powerful. That is bad news for any theology that thinks it has him measured, including the friends'.

verseByVerse.quote: "With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding. If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open. If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land. With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his.
verseByVerse.commentary:
With God are wisdom and might; he has counsel and understanding. Here is Job's thesis. Not with the old men; with God. And the rest of the chapter is a hymn to prove it.

If he tears down, none can rebuild; if he shuts a man in, none can open. No one reverses God. Isaiah uses these words of a steward given the key of David's house (Isa 22:22), and Jesus takes them as his own title: the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens (Rev 3:7). The one who holds the keys that no one can overrule is Christ, and for his people he holds them open.

If he withholds the waters, they dry up; if he sends them out, they overwhelm the land. Drought and flood are both his. With him are strength and sound wisdom; the deceived and the deceiver are his. Even deception is not outside his rule. The reader thinks at once of the accuser in the council, whom Revelation calls the deceiver of the whole world (Rev 12:9). He too is God's, on God's leash, going only as far as he is let.

verseByVerse.quote: He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools. He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips. He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty. He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders. He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He leads counselors away stripped, and judges he makes fools. He looses the bonds of kings and binds a waistcloth on their hips. He leads priests away stripped and overthrows the mighty. He deprives of speech those who are trusted and takes away the discernment of the elders. He pours contempt on princes and loosens the belt of the strong.

A procession of the great, marched off in shame. Counselors and judges, the clever men, made fools. Kings stripped to a loincloth like captives. Priests led away. Trusted speakers struck dumb. Elders who lose their judgment. It is what happened, again and again, when empires fell and their leaders were paraded as prisoners.

Job's point is aimed at the friends. You think wisdom guarantees your standing? God strips the wise. Paul says the same of every clever system that sets itself up against God: Where is the one who is wise? Where is the scribe? ... Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? (1 Cor 1:20). And the psalmist took two of Job's lines and joined them: he pours contempt on princes and makes them wander in trackless wastes (Ps 107:40; cf. vv. 21, 24).

The picture of the great led away stripped, in shame, is the picture Paul uses for the cross. There the rulers of this age did their worst, and none of the rulers of this age understood this, for if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8). And there God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in him (Col 2:15). The procession Job describes has a victor at its head, and it is Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light. He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away. He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste. They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He uncovers the deeps out of darkness and brings deep darkness to light. The deep darkness Job called down on his birthday (3:5) is the very thing God drags into the daylight. Nothing is hidden from him. That is a warning to the friends, and a promise to Job. Paul turns it on everyone who judges another's heart too soon: do not pronounce judgment before the time, before the Lord comes, who will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness (1 Cor 4:5). The friends have pronounced judgment before the time. God will bring to light what was hidden, and what comes to light will be Job's innocence.

He makes nations great, and he destroys them; he enlarges nations, and leads them away. He takes away understanding from the chiefs of the people of the earth and makes them wander in a trackless waste. They grope in the dark without light, and he makes them stagger like a drunken man. Whole nations rise and fall at his word. Their leaders lose their way and stumble like drunkards, groping in the dark, the curse of Deuteronomy that Eliphaz used against Job (5:14). Job's reply: it falls on kings and nations and wise men too, and you cannot read a man's guilt from it. God rules the whole world. That is exactly why no one can track his ways by counting who is suffering.

13.title: Though He Slay Me
13.text: <sup>1</sup>"Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it.<sup>2</sup>What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you.<sup>3</sup>But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.<sup>4</sup>As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all.<sup>5</sup>Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!<sup>6</sup>Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips.<sup>7</sup>Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him?<sup>8</sup>Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?<sup>9</sup>Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man?<sup>10</sup>He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality.<sup>11</sup>Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you?<sup>12</sup>Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.<sup>13</sup>"Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may.<sup>14</sup>Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?<sup>15</sup>Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.<sup>16</sup>This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.<sup>17</sup>Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears.<sup>18</sup>Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right.<sup>19</sup>Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.<sup>20</sup>Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face:<sup>21</sup>withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me.<sup>22</sup>Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.<sup>23</sup>How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin.<sup>24</sup>Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?<sup>25</sup>Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff?<sup>26</sup>For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.<sup>27</sup>You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet.<sup>28</sup>Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
13.overview: Job knows all the friends know; he wants to argue his case with God. They whitewash with lies and are worthless physicians; silence would be their wisdom. Will they speak falsely for God and plead his case? God will search them out and rebuke them; their maxims are proverbs of ashes (vv. 1-12). Let them be silent while he speaks, whatever comes: though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face. This will be his salvation, for the godless would not come before God; he has prepared his case and knows he is in the right (vv. 13-19). He asks God to take away his hand and his terror and to speak with him; to show him his sin; why does God hide his face and count him an enemy, pursuing a driven leaf, writing bitter things against him, putting his feet in the stocks, as man wastes away like a moth-eaten garment (vv. 20-28)?
13.theology:
God does not need lies told in his defence; the friends' speech is speaking falsely for God, and Job's warning that God will rebuke them is fulfilled (vv. 7-10; 42:7). Job will go to God even at the cost of his life (v. 15), and Paul borrows his words facing death (Phil 1:19-20).

Job's challenge, who will contend with me?, becomes the Servant's (Isa 50:8-9) and the Christian's (Rom 8:33-34). The record written against us has been nailed to the cross (v. 26; Col 2:14).
13.examples:
Plasterers of lies and worthless physicians.

Will you speak falsely for God?: the charge that sums up the friends.

Though he slay me: the Hebrew has a well-known difficulty; the second half stands either way.

Paul borrows verse 16 in prison.

Enemy (oyev) and Job (Iyyov).

The bitter record, and the record nailed to the cross.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Job knows all they know; he would argue his case with God himself (vv. 1-3). You whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all; silence would be their wisdom (vv. 4-6). Will you speak falsely for God? God will search them out and rebuke them (vv. 7-11). Your maxims are proverbs of ashes (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job warns the friends that God will rebuke them for lying on his behalf. At the end, God does exactly that (42:7).

verseByVerse.quote: "Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it. What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, my eye has seen all this, my ear has heard and understood it. What you know, I also know; I am not inferior to you. But I would speak to the Almighty, and I desire to argue my case with God.

Job has heard their theology and knows it well. He is done arguing with them. He wants to argue with God. Argue my case comes from the same Hebrew root as the arbiter of 9:33 and God's own let us reason together (Isa 1:18). Job wants a hearing in the highest court. The friends want to settle his case without one.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all. Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom!
verseByVerse.commentary:
As for you, you whitewash with lies; worthless physicians are you all. Two pictures. Plasterers who smear whitewash over a crumbling wall to hide the cracks: Ezekiel used the same picture for false prophets who cried Peace, when there is no peace, and covered a bad wall with whitewash (Ezek 13:10). And doctors who cannot heal. They came as physicians to a sick man and have made him worse.

There is a Physician who does not fail. Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick (Mark 2:17). He does not whitewash; he heals.

Oh that you would keep silent, and it would be your wisdom! Proverbs says the same, even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise (Prov 17:28). The friends were wisest in the seven days when they said nothing (2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips. Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him? Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear now my argument and listen to the pleadings of my lips. Will you speak falsely for God and speak deceitfully for him? Will you show partiality toward him? Will you plead the case for God?

Here is the charge that sums up the whole book's judgment on the friends. They think they are defending God. To defend him, they have to invent guilt in Job. They are telling lies on God's behalf, taking his side like a bribed witness, pleading his case as if he needed a lawyer.

God does not need lies told for him. Every attempt to protect God's reputation by bending the truth about a sufferer is this sin. A pastor who says "this must be for something you did" without knowing it, to keep his theology tidy, is speaking falsely for God.

verseByVerse.quote: Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man? He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality. Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you? Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will it be well with you when he searches you out? Or can you deceive him, as one deceives a man? He will surely rebuke you if in secret you show partiality. Will not his majesty terrify you, and the dread of him fall upon you?

Job warns them: God searches hearts, and he will not be flattered. You think he is on your side because you are taking his side? He will rebuke you for it. That is exactly what happens. When God has finished speaking to Job, he turns to Eliphaz: My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has (42:7). Job knew God better than they did. He knew God would not thank anyone for lying in his defence.

Your maxims are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are defenses of clay. Job sits in the ashes, and their sayings are ash too: dry, weightless, blown away. Their arguments are walls of clay that crumble at a touch.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Let them be silent; he will speak, whatever comes (vv. 13-14). Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face (v. 15). This will be my salvation (v. 16). I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right (vv. 17-19).
verseByVerse.theology: Job will go to God though it kills him, sure that the godless could not come before him. Paul took his words into prison with him (Phil 1:19-20).

verseByVerse.quote: "Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may. Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let me have silence, and I will speak, and let come on me what may. Why should I take my flesh in my teeth and put my life in my hand?

Be quiet and let me speak to God, whatever happens. To put my life in my hand is to risk everything, as Jephthah said when he went out to battle (Judg 12:3). Job knows that bringing his case before God may cost him his life. He is going to do it anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though he slay me, I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face.

These are some of the best-loved words in the book, and the reader should know that the Hebrew has a well-known difficulty. The consonants of the text read not; the scribes who handed it down noted in the margin that it was to be read in him, two words that sound the same in Hebrew. The ESV follows the margin: though he slay me, I will hope in him. Read the other way, it says: he will kill me; I have no hope; but I will still argue my ways to his face.

Either way, the second half stands, and it is the heart of the verse. Job will go to God. Even if it kills him, he will not turn away from God to anyone else. That is the answer to Satan's question at its sharpest: here is a man with nothing left to gain from God, not even his life, who still insists on God. On the ESV's reading it is more than that: it is hope that looks through death to God himself.

The Christian says it with more light. Jesus, dying, said Father, into your hands I commit my spirit! (Luke 23:46). The Father did let him die, and he hoped in him, and was raised. Because of that, a believer can say Job's words on his own deathbed and mean them fully.

verseByVerse.quote: This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This will be my salvation, that the godless shall not come before him.

Job's confidence is this: a godless man would never dare to come before God to have his case heard. The fact that Job wants nothing more than to stand before God is itself the sign that he is not godless. His salvation here means his rescue, his vindication.

Paul knew this verse. Writing from prison, not knowing whether he would be executed, he borrows the words of the Greek Old Testament almost exactly: this will turn out for my deliverance, and goes straight on to Job's hope in the face of death, that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death (Phil 1:19-20). The apostle read himself into Job's place: a righteous man in chains, sure that God would vindicate him, whether he lived or died.

verseByVerse.quote: Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears. Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right. Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Keep listening to my words, and let my declaration be in your ears. Behold, I have prepared my case; I know that I shall be in the right. Who is there who will contend with me? For then I would be silent and die.

Job has his case ready. He is sure of the verdict. If anyone can prove the charge against him, he will fall silent and die. It is a bold claim, and Job will have to learn that being in the right about his innocence is not the same as being in the right about God (40:8). But he is not wrong that no charge will stand.

Listen to how these words sound again in Isaiah, on the lips of the Servant of the LORD, beaten and spat upon: He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? ... Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up (Isa 50:8-9). The same challenge, and the same moth-eaten garment that ends this chapter (v. 28). And Paul takes the Servant's words and hands them to every Christian: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn? Christ Jesus is the one who died (Rom 8:33-34). Job's lonely defiance became the Servant's confidence, and the Servant's confidence became ours.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–28 — Why Do You Hide Your Face?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two requests: take your hand away, and let not dread terrify me; then call, and I will answer (vv. 20-22). Make me know my transgression and my sin. Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy? (vv. 23-24). God pursues a driven leaf, writes bitter things against him, puts his feet in the stocks; man wastes away like a moth-eaten garment (vv. 25-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks to see the charge sheet. The Christian knows where the record against him went: nailed to the cross (Col 2:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only grant me two things, then I will not hide myself from your face: withdraw your hand far from me, and let not dread of you terrify me. Then call, and I will answer; or let me speak, and you reply to me.

Now Job turns from the friends and speaks to God. He makes the same two requests as at 9:34: take your hand off me, and do not overwhelm me with terror. Then let us talk. You speak first and I will answer, or I will speak and you answer.

God will take the first option. When he speaks from the whirlwind he says, I will question you, and you make it known to me (38:3). And Job will find that he has nothing to answer. The hearing he longs for will not go the way he imagines. It will be better.

verseByVerse.quote: How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin. Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy?
verseByVerse.commentary:
How many are my iniquities and my sins? Make me know my transgression and my sin. Show me the list. If I have sinned, name it. It is the prayer of an honest man, and every believer can pray it: Search me, O God, and know my heart (Ps 139:23). Job is not hiding from any sin he might have. He cannot find one that explains this.

Why do you hide your face and count me as your enemy? The hidden face is the deepest pain in the psalms: How long will you hide your face from me? (Ps 13:1). And there is a play on words here that a Hebrew reader would hear. Enemy is oyev; Job's name is Iyyov. Why do you treat Job as if he were your enemy?

The gospel turns the question round. God did count us as enemies, and we were: while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son (Rom 5:10). Job was not God's enemy, and felt treated as one. Christ was not God's enemy, and was treated as one, so that God's real enemies could be made his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff? For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Will you frighten a driven leaf and pursue dry chaff? I am a dead leaf in the wind, a bit of chaff. Why would the Almighty chase something so small? The picture comes from the covenant curses: the sound of a driven leaf shall put them to flight (Lev 26:36). Again Job feels treated as one of the cursed.
