For you write bitter things against me and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth. God seems to be writing up a charge sheet, bitter entries, and adding to it the sins of Job's young days. Job does not deny that he sinned as a young man. He asks why old, forgiven sins should be brought up now. David prayed, Remember not the sins of my youth (Ps 25:7).

There was a written record against us, and it was real. Paul tells us what God did with it: canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross (Col 2:14). The bitter things written against the believer are not being added to. They have been nailed up and cancelled.

verseByVerse.quote: You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet. Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You put my feet in the stocks and watch all my paths; you set a limit for the soles of my feet. A prisoner in the stocks, every step watched, a line drawn round his feet that he may not cross. That is how his illness feels: confinement. Paul and Silas once sat with their feet in the stocks in a Philippian jail, and at midnight they were praying and singing hymns to God (Acts 16:24-25). The stocks do not have the last word over God's people.

Man wastes away like a rotten thing, like a garment that is moth-eaten. Job ends by looking at himself: rotting like old wood, full of holes like a moth-eaten coat. It is the bridge to chapter 14, where he will think about every human life. And it is the image the Servant uses, not of himself, but of his accusers: the moth will eat them up (Isa 50:9).

14.title: If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
14.text: <sup>1</sup>"Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble.<sup>2</sup>He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.<sup>3</sup>And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you?<sup>4</sup>Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.<sup>5</sup>Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass,<sup>6</sup>look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.<sup>7</sup>"For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease.<sup>8</sup>Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil,<sup>9</sup>yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.<sup>10</sup>But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he?<sup>11</sup>As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up,<sup>12</sup>so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.<sup>13</sup>Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!<sup>14</sup>If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.<sup>15</sup>You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands.<sup>16</sup>For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin;<sup>17</sup>my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.<sup>18</sup>"But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place;<sup>19</sup>the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.<sup>20</sup>You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away.<sup>21</sup>His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not.<sup>22</sup>He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
14.overview: Man born of woman is few of days and full of trouble, a withering flower, a passing shadow; why bring him to judgment, when no one can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? His days are determined; let God look away and give him rest (vv. 1-6). There is hope for a tree, which sprouts again from its stump; but a man dies and does not rise till the heavens are no more (vv. 7-12). Oh that God would hide him in Sheol until his wrath is past and then remember him! If a man dies, shall he live again? He would wait all his service for his relief; God would call and he would answer, and God would cover his sin (vv. 13-17). But as water wears stone, God destroys the hope of man; he goes away, knows nothing of his sons, and feels only his own pain (vv. 18-22).
14.theology:
No one born of woman is clean (v. 4; Ps 51:5), except the one born of woman who was holy (Gal 4:4; Luke 1:35). The first flash of resurrection hope in the book (vv. 13-17) is answered in Christ, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20), whose voice all in the tombs will hear (John 5:28).

Job's hope to have his sin covered uses the word for the friends' whitewash (13:4): they plaster lies over truth; God covers sin (Ps 32:1).
14.examples:
Born of a woman: Galatians 4:4.

There is not one, until the child who was called holy.

A shoot from the stump: Isaiah 11:1.

Till the heavens are no more: Scripture gives the date.

The soldier on watch waits for his relief.

You would call, and I would answer you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Few of Days and Full of Trouble
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble, a flower that withers, a passing shadow (vv. 1-2). Why bring such a one into judgment? Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one (vv. 3-4). His days are numbered; let God look away and give him his day's rest (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job speaks for every human being: short-lived, troubled, unclean. The Son of God was born of woman (Gal 4:4), and he alone was holy.

verseByVerse.quote: "Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble. He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Man who is born of a woman is few of days and full of trouble. He comes out like a flower and withers; he flees like a shadow and continues not.

Job widens his view from himself to every human being. Born of a woman: weak, mortal, sharing the lot of all flesh. Few of days: life is short. Full of trouble: the word is the last word of chapter 3, trouble comes (3:26). A flower opens in the morning and is wilted by evening; a shadow slides across the ground and is gone.

Isaiah heard the same and added what Job could not yet say: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever (Isa 40:8), and Peter tells the church that this word is the gospel (1 Pet 1:25). And there is a greater answer in the first phrase. When the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman (Gal 4:4). The Son of God took on the short, troubled life that Job describes, so that those born of women could be born of God.

verseByVerse.quote: And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you? Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And do you open your eyes on such a one and bring me into judgment with you? Why would the Almighty fix his eyes on something as brief as a man and haul him into court? It is the complaint of 7:17-19 again: God's attention feels like prosecution.

Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean? There is not one. Job knows that no one born of a woman is pure. Sin runs in the stock. David said it of himself: in sin did my mother conceive me (Ps 51:5). Job is not claiming to be sinless; he is saying that if God demands perfect cleanness, no human being could ever pass.

And yet once, one clean thing did come out of the unclean. The angel said to Mary, the child to be born will be called holy — the Son of God (Luke 1:35). Job's there is not one was true of every child ever born, until that one. He is the only man who could stand God's scrutiny, and he stood it for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass, look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Since his days are determined, and the number of his months is with you, and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass, look away from him and leave him alone, that he may enjoy, like a hired hand, his day.

God has fixed the length of every life. Job does not dispute it; the psalmist rejoiced in it: My times are in your hand (Ps 31:15). Job's plea is only: since my days are already counted and few, let me have them in peace. Give me what a hired labourer gets at the end of his shift, a little rest before the day is over (7:1-2).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — There Is Hope for a Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: There is hope for a tree: cut down, it sprouts again at the scent of water (vv. 7-9). But a man dies and is laid low; like a dried-up river, he lies down and does not rise till the heavens are no more (vv. 10-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job sees more hope for a stump than for a man. God's answer is a shoot from a stump (Isa 11:1), and a day when the heavens will pass away and the sleepers wake.

verseByVerse.quote: "For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease. Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil, yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there is hope for a tree, if it be cut down, that it will sprout again, and that its shoots will not cease. Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stump die in the soil, yet at the scent of water it will bud and put out branches like a young plant.

Anyone who has cut down a tree and seen green shoots come up from the stump the next spring knows the picture. The trunk is gone, the stump looks dead, and then after rain it sends up new growth. Hope is the word Job said his life had run out of (7:6). A tree has it. Has a man?

God's own answer to that question came as a stump. Isaiah foresaw the royal line of David cut down to a stump, and promised, There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit (Isa 11:1). The Messiah came up out of a dead stump, and he himself was cut down and came up again from the grave. There is hope for a tree; there is more for a man in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he? As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up, so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But a man dies and is laid low; man breathes his last, and where is he? As waters fail from a lake and a river wastes away and dries up, so a man lies down and rises not again; till the heavens are no more he will not awake or be roused out of his sleep.

A man is not like the tree. He breathes his last and is gone. Where is he? He is like a lake that drains away in the summer heat, and there is no spring rain for him. Job sees death as a sleep with no waking.

But look at the phrase he uses: till the heavens are no more. Job means "never". Scripture takes him at his word and gives it a date. The heavens will pass away with a roar (2 Pet 3:10); John saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away (Rev 21:1). There will be a day when the heavens are no more, and on that day the sleepers wake. Jesus called death sleep in the same way, and meant it hopefully: Our friend Lazarus has fallen asleep, but I go to awaken him (John 11:11).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — If a Man Dies, Shall He Live Again?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Oh that you would hide me in Sheol ... until your wrath be past ... and remember me! (v. 13). If a man dies, shall he live again? He would wait all his service for his relief (v. 14). God would call and he would answer; God would long for the work of his hands, and cover over his sin (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: The first flash of resurrection hope in the book. Jesus says the hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice (John 5:28).

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!
verseByVerse.commentary:
Oh that you would hide me in Sheol, that you would conceal me until your wrath be past, that you would appoint me a set time, and remember me!

Here the hope breaks through. Job imagines the grave not as the end but as a hiding place, where God keeps him safe until the storm of wrath has passed, and then sets a day to come and get him. Remember me. Isaiah uses the same picture for God's people: hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by (Isa 26:20).

The Christian knows where that hiding place is: your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col 3:3). And he knows the answer to remember me. A dying thief on a cross said it, Jesus, remember me when you come into your kingdom (Luke 23:42), and was told, today you will be with me in paradise.

verseByVerse.quote: If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If a man dies, shall he live again? All the days of my service I would wait, till my renewal should come.

The great question, asked honestly. It is not answered in this chapter, and it is not a statement of doctrine; it is a man daring to hope. But look at what he says next. My service is the word of 7:1, the soldier's hard service. There it was hopeless drudgery. Here it is a soldier on sentry duty waiting for his relief. Renewal means exactly that: the change of guard, the fresh man who comes to take over. Job imagines lying in the grave as on a long watch, waiting to be relieved.

The New Testament answers his question with a person. Christ has been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep (1 Cor 15:20). And Paul uses Job's idea of change: we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet (1 Cor 15:51-52). The relief Job waited for is coming, and it will come with a trumpet.

verseByVerse.quote: You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands. For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin; my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
You would call, and I would answer you; you would long for the work of your hands.

This is the tenderest line Job has spoken. God would call to him out of the grave, and he would answer. And God would long for him, as a craftsman misses the work he made (10:3, 8). Job imagines God missing him. Jesus said it would happen: an hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out (John 5:28-29).

For then you would number my steps; you would not keep watch over my sin; my transgression would be sealed up in a bag, and you would cover over my iniquity. In that day God would still watch his steps, but as a father watches a child walk, not as a guard watches a prisoner. His sins would be sealed in a bag, like a legal document tied and sealed and put away, never to be opened again.

And cover over is a striking word. It is the verb of 13:4, where Job said the friends whitewash with lies: plaster smeared over cracks. The friends plaster lies over the truth about Job. Job hopes that God will plaster over the truth about his sin, cover it so it is seen no more. That is the gospel's own hope: Blessed is the one whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered (Ps 32:1). You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (Mic 7:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — You Destroy the Hope of Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: As water wears away stone, so you destroy the hope of man (vv. 18-19). God prevails and sends him away; his sons are honoured or brought low and he never knows; he feels only his own pain (vv. 20-22).
verseByVerse.theology: The hope flickers and goes out again. It will come back stronger (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place; the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But the mountain falls and crumbles away, and the rock is removed from its place; the waters wear away the stones; the torrents wash away the soil of the earth; so you destroy the hope of man.

Then the light goes out again. Even mountains crumble; running water grinds stone smooth and carries the soil away. Hope is worn down the same way, slowly and completely.

This is how faith often moves in real suffering. A flash of hope, like verses 13-17, and then the old grief rolls back in. The believer should not despise the flash because it did not last. Job's hope will come back, steadier, five chapters on: I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away. His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not. He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
You prevail forever against him, and he passes; you change his countenance, and send him away. His sons come to honor, and he does not know it; they are brought low, and he perceives it not. He feels only the pain of his own body, and he mourns only for himself.

Death changes a man's face and sends him out of the world. Whatever becomes of his children, honour or disgrace, he will never know; the dead know nothing, as the Preacher says (Eccl 9:5). Read these lines as the words of a man whose sons are all dead. He would give anything to know anything about them.

The speech ends in pain: the dead feel only their own body, mourn only for themselves. It is the bleakest ending yet. But the reader has already heard, in the middle of the chapter, a man imagining God calling him out of the grave. That call was not imagination. Christ has been raised from the dead (1 Cor 15:20), and the voice that will call is his.

15.title: Have You Listened in the Council of God?
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind?<sup>3</sup>Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good?<sup>4</sup>But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God.<sup>5</sup>For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty.<sup>6</sup>Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.<sup>7</sup>"Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills?<sup>8</sup>Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?<sup>9</sup>What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us?<sup>10</sup>Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father.<sup>11</sup>Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you?<sup>12</sup>Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash,<sup>13</sup>that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?<sup>14</sup>What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous?<sup>15</sup>Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight;<sup>16</sup>how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!<sup>17</sup>"I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare<sup>18</sup>(what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers,<sup>19</sup>to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).<sup>20</sup>The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless.<sup>21</sup>Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him.<sup>22</sup>He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword.<sup>23</sup>He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand;<sup>24</sup>distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.<sup>25</sup>Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty,<sup>26</sup>running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield;<sup>27</sup>because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist<sup>28</sup>and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins;<sup>29</sup>he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth;<sup>30</sup>he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.<sup>31</sup>Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment.<sup>32</sup>It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green.<sup>33</sup>He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree.<sup>34</sup>For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.<sup>35</sup>They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
15.overview: Eliphaz opens the second round without courtesy: Job's words are wind; he is doing away with the fear of God; his own mouth condemns him (vv. 1-6). Is Job the first man born? Has he listened in the council of God? The grey-haired side with the friends; are the comforts of God too small for him (vv. 7-13)? No man is pure, least of all one who drinks injustice like water (vv. 14-16). Eliphaz declares what the wise have handed down: the wicked man lives in dread, the destroyer comes in his prosperity, because he defied the Almighty; his wealth will not last, the flame dries his shoots, he is shaken off like an unripe grape; the company of the godless is barren and fire consumes their tents (vv. 17-35).
15.theology:
The second round turns to one subject, the fate of the wicked (chs 15, 18, 20), and every detail fits Job's own losses, so that the portrait of the wicked becomes a portrait of the innocent. God judged the speech false (42:7).

Eliphaz mocks the idea that Job has listened in God's council; the reader has, and it vindicates Job. Christ, the firstborn of all creation, has made the Father known (Col 1:15; John 1:18), and was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37).
15.examples:
The courtesy of chapter 4 is gone.

Have you listened in the council of God? The reader has.

Eliphaz calls his speeches the comforts of God.

The fate of the wicked, told in the details of Job's own losses.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz calls Job's words wind and says he is doing away with the fear of God; his own mouth condemns him (vv. 1-6). Are you the first man who was born? ... Have you listened in the council of God? The grey-haired are on the friends' side (vv. 7-10). Are the comforts of God too small for you? (vv. 11-13). No man is pure; God does not trust even his holy ones, much less one who is abominable and corrupt (vv. 14-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The second round begins with the courtesy gone. Eliphaz mocks the idea that Job has heard the council of God. The reader has heard it, and it convicts Eliphaz.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said: "Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? Should he argue in unprofitable talk, or in words with which he can do no good? But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God. For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second round of speeches begins, and it follows the first. The friends' case was set out in chapters 4-5, 8 and 11, and the reader should hold on to the LORD's verdict on it: you have not spoken of me what is right (42:7). What is new in round two is the tone, and the subject.

The tone first. Eliphaz began chapter 4 by asking permission to speak. Now: Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge, and fill his belly with the east wind? The east wind is the scorching desert wind, hot and useless. But you are doing away with the fear of God and hindering meditation before God. Job's talk, he says, is destroying piety itself. And yet the fear of God was the very thing God praised in Job (1:1, 8).

Your own mouth condemns you, and not I; your own lips testify against you. Job had said, though I am in the right, my own mouth would condemn me (9:20), meaning that God would twist his words. Eliphaz takes Job's fear and makes it his verdict. It is a common move in any quarrel, and a cruel one in pastoral care: to take what a grieving person says in anguish and use it as evidence against him.

verseByVerse.quote: "Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills? Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself? What do you know that we do not know? What do you understand that is not clear to us? Both the gray-haired and the aged are among us, older than your father. Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you? Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash, that you turn your spirit against God and bring such words out of your mouth?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Are you the first man who was born? Or were you brought forth before the hills? Have you listened in the council of God? And do you limit wisdom to yourself?

Eliphaz mocks: who do you think you are, the first man ever made, older than the hills, a member of God's private council? Here is the sharpest irony in the round. The reader has listened in the council of God. Chapters 1 and 2 took us there, and what was said there was that Job was blameless and that his suffering was without reason (2:3). Eliphaz mocks the one source that could settle the argument, and it is against him.

The words brought forth before the hills are those of Wisdom in Proverbs: before the hills, I was brought forth (Prov 8:25). No mere man was there. But one was. The New Testament calls Christ the firstborn of all creation (Col 1:15), the only Son who is at the Father's side (John 1:18). He has listened in the council of God, and he has told us what is in the Father's heart. God himself will use Eliphaz's irony on Job, gently: You know, for you were born then (38:21).

Are the comforts of God too small for you, or the word that deals gently with you? This is what Eliphaz calls his own speeches: God's comforts, spoken gently. Job's answer will come in the next chapter: miserable comforters are you all (16:2). The test of comfort is not what the comforter calls it.

verseByVerse.quote: What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous? Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight; how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!
verseByVerse.commentary:
What is man, that he can be pure? Or he who is born of a woman, that he can be righteous? Behold, God puts no trust in his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure in his sight; how much less one who is abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water!

This is Eliphaz's night vision again, in the same shape and many of the same words (4:17-19); what was said about it there applies here. What is new is where it lands. In chapter 4 the vision spoke of mortals in general. Now the last line is aimed: abominable and corrupt, a man who drinks injustice like water. Eliphaz has moved from "no one is pure" to "you are foul". That is the whole slide of the friends' argument in one sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–35 — The Wicked Man Writhes in Pain
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eliphaz will declare what the wise have handed down (vv. 17-19). The wicked man lives in dread; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him (vv. 20-24), because he defied the Almighty (vv. 25-28). His wealth will not last; the flame will dry up his shoots (vv. 29-30); he is shaken off like an unripe grape (vv. 31-33); the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery (vv. 34-35).
verseByVerse.theology: The subject of the whole second round, the fate of the wicked, and every detail is a line from Job's own story in chapter 1.

verseByVerse.quote: "I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare (what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers, to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).
verseByVerse.commentary:
I will show you; hear me, and what I have seen I will declare (what wise men have told, without hiding it from their fathers, to whom alone the land was given, and no stranger passed among them).

Eliphaz appeals again to what he has seen and to the tradition of the fathers, pure and unmixed, handed down in a land no foreigner entered. Bildad made the same appeal (8:8-10). The trouble is not that tradition is worthless. It is that no tradition, however pure, knew what happened in the council of God about this man.

verseByVerse.quote: The wicked man writhes in pain all his days, through all the years that are laid up for the ruthless. Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him. He does not believe that he will return out of darkness, and he is marked for the sword. He wanders abroad for bread, saying, 'Where is it?' He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand; distress and anguish terrify him; they prevail against him, like a king ready for battle.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here begins the new subject of the second round. All three friends will now preach the same sermon: the terrible end of the wicked (15:20-35; 18:5-21; 20:4-29). No more promises of restoration; only warning.

The wicked man writhes in pain all his days ... Dreadful sounds are in his ears; in prosperity the destroyer will come upon him. He lives in dread; he is marked for the sword; he wanders looking for bread; distress closes on him like a king ready for battle.

Every reader of chapter 1 knows who this describes. A man at the height of his prosperity, and the destroyer came. The sword fell on his servants (1:15, 17). He is in pain every day. Eliphaz never names Job. He does not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty, running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield; because he has covered his face with his fat and gathered fat upon his waist and has lived in desolate cities, in houses that none should inhabit, which were ready to become heaps of ruins; he will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure, nor will his possessions spread over the earth; he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots, and by the breath of his mouth he will depart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because he has stretched out his hand against God and defies the Almighty, running stubbornly against him with a thickly bossed shield; because he has covered his face with his fat. This is the reason Eliphaz gives: the wicked man charges at God like a soldier with a studded shield, grown fat and arrogant, like Israel who grew fat, and kicked (Deut 32:15).

But stretched out his hand against God turns the prologue upside down. In chapter 1 it was Satan who asked God to stretch out your hand against Job (1:11). Job has not raised his hand against God. He has kept his hands open to him, even in protest.

He will not be rich, and his wealth will not endure ... he will not depart from darkness; the flame will dry up his shoots. The wealth that did not endure; the fire of God that fell on his flocks (1:16). It is Job's story, told as a sinner's fate.

verseByVerse.quote: Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself, for emptiness will be his payment. It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green. He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree. For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery. They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
It will be paid in full before his time, and his branch will not be green. He will shake off his unripe grape like the vine, and cast off his blossom like the olive tree. For the company of the godless is barren, and fire consumes the tents of bribery.

The vine that drops its grapes before they ripen; the olive that sheds its blossom: children lost before they grew old, a house left barren. Eliphaz has chosen the image of fruit that dies young to describe the wicked, in front of a man whose ten children died young.

They conceive trouble and give birth to evil, and their womb prepares deceit. The psalmist says the same of the wicked (Ps 7:14), and it is true of them. It is not true of Job.

There is one man of whom every line of this chapter was said, and it was all false. He was counted among the wicked. Jesus said, this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: And he was numbered with the transgressors (Luke 22:37; Isa 53:12). The innocent one was treated as the man Eliphaz describes, so that the guilty could be treated as innocent.

16.title: My Witness Is in Heaven
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all.<sup>3</sup>Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?<sup>4</sup>I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you.<sup>5</sup>I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.<sup>6</sup>"If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me?<sup>7</sup>Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company.<sup>8</sup>And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.<sup>9</sup>He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me.<sup>10</sup>Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me.<sup>11</sup>God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.<sup>12</sup>I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target;<sup>13</sup>his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground.<sup>14</sup>He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.<sup>15</sup>I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust.<sup>16</sup>My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness,<sup>17</sup>although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.<sup>18</sup>"O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.<sup>19</sup>Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.<sup>20</sup>My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God,<sup>21</sup>that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor.<sup>22</sup>For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
16.overview: Job calls the friends miserable comforters with windy words; if they were in his place he could mock them, or strengthen them (vv. 1-5). His pain goes on whether he speaks or not. God has worn him out, torn him in wrath and handed him over to the wicked; men strike his cheek; God set him up as a target and ran at him like a warrior. He sits in sackcloth, his face red with weeping, though there is no violence in his hands and his prayer is pure (vv. 6-17). Let the earth not cover his blood. Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven; with tears he asks God to plead a man's case with God, as a son of man pleads for his neighbour, for his years are few (vv. 18-22).
16.theology:
Job's description of his suffering (vv. 9-11, 17) is the language of the suffering Servant (Isa 50:6; 53:9) and of the passion of Christ (Matt 26:67; Acts 2:23): innocent, struck, handed over, although there is no violence in my hands.

From no arbiter (9:33) Job climbs to my witness is in heaven (v. 19), one who pleads with God as a son of man for his neighbour (v. 21). Christ is the faithful witness and advocate (Rev 1:5; 1 John 2:1), and his blood speaks a better word than Abel's (Heb 12:24).
16.examples:
Miserable comforters: comforters of trouble.

The same mouth can mock or strengthen.

Struck on the cheek, handed over to the wicked.

No violence in my hands: Isaiah 53:9.

O earth, cover not my blood: Abel, and the better blood.

Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all (vv. 1-2). Their words are wind (v. 3). If they were in his place, he could shake his head at them, or he could strengthen them (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Eliphaz called his speeches the comforts of God (15:11). Job calls them what they are. He knows what real comfort would sound like, because he used to give it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all. Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: I have heard many such things; miserable comforters are you all. Shall windy words have an end? Or what provokes you that you answer?

Eliphaz had called his speeches the comforts of God (15:11). Job answers with the most famous description of the friends in the book: miserable comforters, literally comforters of trouble, the word Job has used for his life since chapter 3. They came to comfort (2:11) and have added to his trouble. And he throws back Eliphaz's opening insult (15:2): whose words are wind now?

Every church needs to hear this, because it is possible to arrive with good intentions and the right doctrines and still be a miserable comforter. The friends were not bad men. They were men who talked when they should have listened, and explained when they should have wept.

verseByVerse.quote: I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you. I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I also could speak as you do, if you were in my place; I could join words together against you and shake my head at you. I could strengthen you with my mouth, and the solace of my lips would assuage your pain.

Swap places, says Job, and I could do what you are doing: string together sermons and shake my head at your misfortune. Or I could do something else: strengthen you, comfort you, ease your pain. He had done exactly that for others (4:3-4). The same mouth can do either. Jesus put it in one sentence: whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them (Matt 7:12).

Shake my head is the gesture of scorn. All who see me mock me ... they wag their heads, says the sufferer of Psalm 22 (Ps 22:7), and at the cross those who passed by derided him, wagging their heads (Matt 27:39).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–17 — He Has Torn Me in His Wrath
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Speaking or silent, his pain goes on (v. 6). God has worn him out and shrivelled him (vv. 7-8), torn him in wrath; men gape at him and strike his cheek, and God has handed him over to the wicked (vv. 9-11). God broke him, set him up as a target, slashed him open, ran at him like a warrior (vv. 12-14). He sits in sackcloth with his face red from weeping, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure (vv. 15-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's suffering is described in the words the prophets would use for the suffering of the Servant, and the Gospels for the passion of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: "If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me? Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company. And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face.
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I speak, my pain is not assuaged, and if I forbear, how much of it leaves me? Talking does not help; silence does not help. Anyone in chronic pain knows the trap.

Surely now God has worn me out; he has made desolate all my company. And he has shriveled me up, which is a witness against me, and my leanness has risen up against me; it testifies to my face. His family is gone, his friends have turned, and his wasted body stands up in court as a witness against him. People look at how thin and sick he is and conclude that he must be guilty. That is the false witness. The true one comes at verse 19.

verseByVerse.quote: He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me. Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me. God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has torn me in his wrath and hated me; he has gnashed his teeth at me; my adversary sharpens his eyes against me. Men have gaped at me with their mouth; they have struck me insolently on the cheek; they mass themselves together against me. God gives me up to the ungodly and casts me into the hands of the wicked.

Job believes God has become his enemy, tearing him like a wild beast, glaring at him. My adversary: Job means God. The reader knows there is another adversary in this story, the one in the council, and that God has not become Job's enemy at all.

Now read these lines slowly, because they will be heard again. Mouths gaping at him, like a ravening and roaring lion (Ps 22:13). Struck on the cheek: with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek (Mic 5:1); I gave ... my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isa 50:6). In the high priest's house they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67). And God gives me up to the ungodly: Peter said of Jesus that he was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God and killed by the hands of lawless men (Acts 2:23). Job's night is a shadow thrown backwards from Good Friday.

verseByVerse.quote: I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target; his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground. He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I was at ease, and he broke me apart; he seized me by the neck and dashed me to pieces; he set me up as his target; his archers surround me. He slashes open my kidneys and does not spare; he pours out my gall on the ground. He breaks me with breach upon breach; he runs upon me like a warrior.

I was at ease: the prosperous life of chapter 1, and then, without warning, everything broken. Job piles up pictures of violence: a man grabbed by the neck and smashed, a target ringed by archers (6:4; 7:20), a wall breached again and again, a soldier charging. The poet of Lamentations felt the same arrows: He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver (Lam 3:13). This is how undeserved suffering feels from the inside. The book lets him say it all, and does not ask the reader to pretend it is anything but agony.

verseByVerse.quote: I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust. My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have sewed sackcloth upon my skin and have laid my strength in the dust. My face is red with weeping, and on my eyelids is deep darkness. The sackcloth is stitched on, as if it has grown into his skin; his strength, literally his horn, the symbol of dignity, is down in the dirt. His eyes are swollen and dark from crying. The horn is how Scripture pictures strength and honour; Hannah sang, my horn is exalted in the LORD (1 Sam 2:1). Job's is in the dust. And the answer, when it came, came as a horn: God has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of his servant David (Luke 1:69).

Although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure.

This is the line to hold on to. Job is suffering like a criminal, and he has done no violence. Isaiah uses the same words of the Servant of the LORD, led to death like a lamb: they made his grave with the wicked ... although he had done no violence, and there was no deceit in his mouth (Isa 53:9). The Hebrew is built the same way. What Job could say of himself in part, the Servant could say perfectly. Job's hands were clean of violence; Christ's were clean of every sin, and they were nailed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–22 — My Witness Is in Heaven
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: O earth, cover not my blood (v. 18). Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high (v. 19). His friends scorn him; he weeps to God that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor (vv. 20-21), for his years are few (v. 22).
verseByVerse.theology: The second step up the ladder: from no arbiter (9:33) to a witness in heaven. The Christian knows his name: Jesus Christ, the faithful witness (Rev 1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place. Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.
verseByVerse.commentary:
O earth, cover not my blood, and let my cry find no resting place.

Job expects to die unjustly, and he asks the ground not to soak up his blood and hide it. Let it lie there and cry out, the way Abel's blood cried from the ground after his brother killed him: The voice of your brother's blood is crying to me from the ground (Gen 4:10). Innocent blood calls for justice. Hebrews speaks of another blood that cries out, and says something better: the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel (Heb 12:24). Abel's blood cried for vengeance. Christ's cries for pardon.

Even now, behold, my witness is in heaven, and he who testifies for me is on high.

Here is the second step. In chapter 9 Job said there was no arbiter between him and God (9:33). Now, in the middle of a chapter as dark as any he has spoken, he says: even now, there is a witness for me in heaven. Someone up there knows the truth and will speak for me.

Who? Many readers think Job means God himself: he appeals to God against God, to the God who knows his innocence against the God who seems to be attacking him. Others think he means a heavenly advocate distinct from God. The New Testament shows how both can be true. God the Son, who is God, stands before the Father for us: Jesus Christ the faithful witness (Rev 1:5), who always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25). Job reached into heaven in the dark and found someone there. He was right.

verseByVerse.quote: My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God, that he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor. For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My friends scorn me; my eye pours out tears to God. The friends scorn; the tears go to God. The Hebrew word for those who scorn can also mean spokesmen or interpreters; it is the word Elihu will use for a mediator (33:23). Job's would-be spokesmen have become his mockers, so he weeps upward.

That he would argue the case of a man with God, as a son of man does with his neighbor. He wants his heavenly witness to plead for him before God the way one man stands up for his neighbour in court. Listen to the phrase: as a son of man. Job longs for an advocate who is on God's side of the courtroom and pleads like one of us. The Son of Man is exactly that: we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).

For when a few years have come I shall go the way from which I shall not return. He is running out of time. He needs the witness to speak soon. The Christian's advocate is speaking now.

17.title: Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
17.text: <sup>1</sup>"My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me.<sup>2</sup>Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.<sup>3</sup>"Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me?<sup>4</sup>Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph.<sup>5</sup>He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.<sup>6</sup>"He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit.<sup>7</sup>My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.<sup>8</sup>The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless.<sup>9</sup>Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger.<sup>10</sup>But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.<sup>11</sup>My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart.<sup>12</sup>They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'<sup>13</sup>If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness,<sup>14</sup>if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,'<sup>15</sup>where then is my hope? Who will see my hope?<sup>16</sup>Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
17.overview: Job's spirit is broken and the grave is ready; mockers surround him. He asks God to lay down a pledge for him with God, for no one else will stand surety for him; God has closed the friends' minds (vv. 1-5). He has become a byword and men spit at him; his body is a shadow. The upright are appalled, yet the righteous holds to his way and grows stronger; there is no wise man among the friends (vv. 6-10). His days are past and his plans broken; the friends call night day. If the grave is his home and the worm his mother, where is his hope? Will it go down to the bars of Sheol (vv. 11-16)?
17.theology:
Job asks God to stand surety for him with God (v. 3), using Judah's word for pledging himself for Benjamin (Gen 43:9). Jesus is the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb 7:22).

The righteous holds to his way even when his spirit is broken (vv. 1, 9): the perseverance of the saints, kept by God. The bars of Sheol (v. 16) are opened by the one who holds the keys of Death (Rev 1:18), and our hope is a living hope (1 Pet 1:3).
17.examples:
Who will put up security for me? Judah for Benjamin; Christ for us.

A byword, and a face spat on.

Yet the righteous holds to his way.

The friends call night day.

The pit my father, the worm my mother.

The bars of Sheol, and the keys.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — Who Will Put Up Security for Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His spirit is broken and the grave is ready; mockers surround him (vv. 1-2). Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me? (v. 3). God has closed the friends' minds; the informer's children will suffer (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: Job asks God to stand surety for him with God. The New Testament names the guarantor: Jesus (Heb 7:22).

verseByVerse.quote: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me. Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
My spirit is broken; my days are extinct; the graveyard is ready for me. Surely there are mockers about me, and my eye dwells on their provocation.

Three short, broken clauses: spirit gone, days snuffed out, the cemetery waiting. It is the voice of a man who expects to die soon. And he cannot even die in peace: mockers stand around him, and he cannot stop seeing their taunts. The friends came to sit with him in grief; now he lies awake with their words in front of his eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: "Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me? Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph. He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property— the eyes of his children will fail.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Lay down a pledge for me with you; who is there who will put up security for me?

This is one of the most remarkable prayers in the book. In the ancient world, when a man could not pay or could not be trusted to appear in court, someone else could stand surety for him: pledge his own property or person as a guarantee, and seal it with a handshake. Job looks around and finds no one who will do it for him. So he asks God himself: you put up the pledge for me, with you. He asks God to stand guarantor for him before God.

The verb is the one Judah used when he offered himself for his brother Benjamin before their father: I will be a pledge of his safety. From my hand you shall require him (Gen 43:9). Judah put his own life on the line for his brother. And the Son of God, of the tribe of Judah, did the same for us. This makes Jesus the guarantor of a better covenant (Heb 7:22). Job asked who would stand surety for him with God. God answered by becoming the surety himself.

Since you have closed their hearts to understanding, therefore you will not let them triumph. He who informs against his friends to get a share of their property — the eyes of his children will fail. God has shut the friends' minds; they will not win this argument. And Job quotes a proverb about the man who betrays his friends for gain: his own children pay for it. The friends have not robbed Job, but they have informed against him to God, and the proverb is a warning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–10 — The Righteous Holds to His Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: He has become a byword, a man people spit at, his body a shadow (vv. 6-7). The upright are appalled; yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger (vv. 8-9). Let them come again; he will find no wise man among them (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: In the middle of his darkest words Job states the perseverance of the saints. The righteous man does not let go.

verseByVerse.quote: "He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit. My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made me a byword of the peoples, and I am one before whom men spit. My eye has grown dim from vexation, and all my members are like a shadow.

A byword is a name people use as a warning: "you'll end up like Job." It is the covenant curse again: you shall become a horror, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples (Deut 28:37). And men spit in his face, the deepest insult in that world. The Servant of the LORD would say, I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting (Isa 50:6), and in the high priest's courtyard they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67). Job's eyes are dim from crying, his body wasted to a shadow.

verseByVerse.quote: The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless. Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger. But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent stirs himself up against the godless. Yet the righteous holds to his way, and he who has clean hands grows stronger and stronger.

Suddenly, in the middle of his lowest words, a burst of steel. Good people look at what has happened to Job and are horrified. But the righteous man does not give up his road. He holds on, and the one with clean hands gets stronger, not weaker, as the pressure grows.

That is what the Reformed churches have called the perseverance of the saints: not that God's people never stumble or despair, but that the one who truly belongs to God holds to his way, because God holds him. The path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, which shines brighter and brighter until full day (Prov 4:18). Job's spirit is broken (v. 1) and his grip on his way is unbroken, both in one chapter. That is exactly what Satan said could not happen.

But you, come on again, all of you, and I shall not find a wise man among you. Try again, all three of you. There is not a wise man in the group.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–16 — Where Then Is My Hope?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: His days are past and his plans broken (v. 11); the friends call the night day (v. 12). If he makes the grave his home, the pit his father and the worm his mother (vv. 13-14), where then is my hope? Will it go down with him to the bars of Sheol (vv. 15-16)?
verseByVerse.theology: Job's hope stands at the gate of the grave. Christ holds its keys (Rev 1:18).

verseByVerse.quote: My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart. They make night into day: 'The light,' they say, 'is near to the darkness.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
My days are past; my plans are broken off, the desires of my heart. Everything he meant to do, everything he hoped for, has been snapped off like thread.

They make night into day: The light, they say, is near to the darkness. This is the friends' cheerful theology. Zophar promised that Job's darkness would be like the morning (11:17). It is midnight, and they keep saying dawn is just round the corner, if only he will repent. It is the false comfort the prophets condemned: They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, Peace, peace, when there is no peace (Jer 6:14). Real comfort does not pretend that night is day. It sits in the night, and waits for the real morning.

verseByVerse.quote: If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness, if I say to the pit, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,' where then is my hope? Who will see my hope? Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
If I hope for Sheol as my house, if I make my bed in darkness, if I say to the pit, You are my father, and to the worm, My mother, or My sister, where then is my hope? Who will see my hope? Will it go down to the bars of Sheol? Shall we descend together into the dust?

If the grave is the only home left to him, and the only family the pit and the worms, then what has become of his hope? Job has lost his father's house and his children. Now he pictures the grave adopting him. And he asks whether his hope will go down with him, through the barred gate of the underworld, and lie in the dust beside him.

The Bible answers with a man who went down to those bars. Jonah prayed from the belly of the fish, To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God (Jonah 2:6), and Jesus called his own death and resurrection the sign of Jonah. The risen Christ says, I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades (Rev 1:18). The bars Job feared are locked from the outside, and Christ has the key.

So Job's question has an answer. Where is my hope? Not in the dust. He has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead (1 Pet 1:3). A hope that has already been through the grave and come out cannot be buried with us.

18.title: The King of Terrors
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak.<sup>3</sup>Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight?<sup>4</sup>You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?<sup>5</sup>"Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine.<sup>6</sup>The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out.<sup>7</sup>His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down.<sup>8</sup>For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh.<sup>9</sup>A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him.<sup>10</sup>A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.<sup>11</sup>Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels.<sup>12</sup>His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling.<sup>13</sup>It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs.<sup>14</sup>He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.<sup>15</sup>In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation.<sup>16</sup>His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above.<sup>17</sup>His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street.<sup>18</sup>He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world.<sup>19</sup>He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.<sup>20</sup>They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east.<sup>21</sup>Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
18.overview: Bildad resents being counted as cattle and asks whether the world should be rearranged for Job (vv. 1-4). The light of the wicked goes out; his own feet lead him into traps; terrors chase him; the firstborn of death consumes his skin and limbs, and he is brought to the king of terrors. Strangers live in his tent, sulfur falls on it, his memory perishes and he has no descendants; east and west are appalled. Such is the place of him who does not know God (vv. 5-21).
18.theology:
Bildad describes the fate of the wicked in the details of Job's own suffering, the skin disease and the lost children, and ends by saying Job does not know God. The LORD judged the speech false (42:7), and Job's answer is I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25).

Death, the king of terrors, has been dethroned: Christ destroyed the one who has the power of death and freed those enslaved by its fear (Heb 2:14-15).
18.examples:
Six words for traps in four verses.

The firstborn of death consumes his limbs, said to a man with a skin disease.

No posterity, said to a father of ten dead children.

Him who knows not God: Job's next words are I know.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Why Are We Counted as Cattle?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How long will you hunt for words? (vv. 1-2). Why does Job treat them as cattle, as stupid (v. 3)? You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you? (v. 4).
verseByVerse.theology: Bildad's pride is hurt, and he tells Job that the world will not be rearranged to suit him.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said: "How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak. Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight? You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bildad speaks again, and the case he set out in chapter 8 has not changed; the subject of this round, the end of the wicked, was set out in chapter 15. What is new here is mostly wounded pride and a sharper picture.

How long will you hunt for words? Consider, and then we will speak. Why are we counted as cattle? Why are we stupid in your sight? Job told them to ask the animals for wisdom (12:7) and said he could not find a wise man among them (17:10). Bildad has taken it personally.

You who tear yourself in your anger, shall the earth be forsaken for you, or the rock be removed out of its place? Job said God had torn him (16:9); Bildad says: you are tearing yourself. And he throws Job's own words back, the rock is removed from its place (14:18): do you expect the world's moral order to be moved for your sake? Bildad is right that God does not rearrange the world to please a sufferer. He has not considered that God's order might be larger than his account of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–21 — The Light of the Wicked Is Put Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lamp of the wicked goes out (vv. 5-6); his own feet walk him into net, trap and snare (vv. 7-10). Terrors chase him; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs, and he is brought to the king of terrors (vv. 11-14). Strangers live in his tent, sulfur falls on it, his roots dry up (vv. 15-16); his memory perishes, he has no descendants (vv. 17-19); east and west are appalled. Such is the place of him who knows not God (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Every line of Bildad's portrait of the wicked describes Job: the skin disease, the lost children, the ruined house. And Job's answer will reach the word Bildad denied him: I know (19:25).

verseByVerse.quote: "Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine. The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out. His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down. For he is cast into a net by his own feet, and he walks on its mesh. A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him. A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Indeed, the light of the wicked is put out, and the flame of his fire does not shine. The light is dark in his tent, and his lamp above him is put out. Proverbs says it too: the lamp of the wicked will be put out (Prov 13:9). Job will remember the days when his lamp shone upon my head (29:3). Bildad says that lamp has gone out because Job is wicked.

His strong steps are shortened, and his own schemes throw him down. For he is cast into a net by his own feet ... A trap seizes him by the heel; a snare lays hold of him. A rope is hidden for him in the ground, a trap for him in the path. Six different words for traps in four verses. The wicked man walks into them by his own steps. It is true of the wicked: in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught (Ps 9:15). But Job did not set these nets. He is caught in something he cannot see, and the reader knows who laid it.

verseByVerse.quote: Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels. His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling. It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs. He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Terrors frighten him on every side, and chase him at his heels. His strength is famished, and calamity is ready for his stumbling. It consumes the parts of his skin; the firstborn of death consumes his limbs.

Here Bildad goes further than he has before. The wicked man, he says, dies of a disease that eats his skin: the firstborn of death, the deadliest sickness there is, death's eldest son. He says this to a man whose skin is crusting and breaking (2:7; 7:5). It is not a general warning any more. It is a diagnosis.

He is torn from the tent in which he trusted and is brought to the king of terrors. Death is pictured as a king, the lord of every fear, and the wicked are marched before him. It is a terrible and true picture of death for those without God. But the New Testament shows the king of terrors dethroned. Christ shared our flesh that through death he might destroy the one who has the power of death, that is, the devil, and deliver all those who through fear of death were subject to lifelong slavery (Heb 2:14-15). The last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Cor 15:26). The believer is not marched before the king of terrors. He is welcomed by the King who conquered him.

verseByVerse.quote: In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation. His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above. His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street. He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world. He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In his tent dwells that which is none of his; sulfur is scattered over his habitation. Strangers move into his house; burning sulfur falls on it, as it fell on Sodom (Gen 19:24). His roots dry up beneath, and his branches wither above. Root and branch: nothing left.

His memory perishes from the earth, and he has no name in the street. He is thrust from light into darkness, and driven out of the world. He has no posterity or progeny among his people, and no survivor where he used to live.

No children, no one to carry his name: Bildad says this to a man whose ten children are in their graves. It is the cruellest turn of his speech. And it is false. Job's name did not perish. Ezekiel named him as a righteous man (Ezek 14:14); James held him up to the church (James 5:11); and his story is read wherever the Bible is read. The righteous ... will be remembered forever (Ps 112:6).

verseByVerse.quote: They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east. Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They of the west are appalled at his day, and horror seizes them of the east. Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous, such is the place of him who knows not God.

Bildad's last line is his verdict: Job is a man who does not know God. The LORD will say otherwise, and Bildad will be among the three he rebukes (42:7-9). And Job's very next speech will reach its peak with the words Bildad has just denied him: For I know that my Redeemer lives (19:25). The man Bildad says does not know God is about to say one of the best-known sentences of faith in the Old Testament.

19.title: I Know That My Redeemer Lives
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Job answered and said:<sup>2</sup>"How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words?<sup>3</sup>These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?<sup>4</sup>And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself.<sup>5</sup>If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me,<sup>6</sup>know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice.<sup>8</sup>He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.<sup>9</sup>He has stripped from me my glory and taken the crown from my head.<sup>10</sup>He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone, and my hope has he pulled up like a tree.<sup>11</sup>He has kindled his wrath against me and counts me as his adversary.<sup>12</sup>His troops come on together; they have cast up their siege ramp against me and encamp around my tent.<sup>13</sup>"He has put my brothers far from me, and those who knew me are wholly estranged from me.<sup>14</sup>My relatives have failed me, my close friends have forgotten me.<sup>15</sup>The guests in my house and my maidservants count me as a stranger; I have become a foreigner in their eyes.<sup>16</sup>I call to my servant, but he gives me no answer; I must plead with him with my mouth for mercy.<sup>17</sup>My breath is strange to my wife, and I am a stench to the children of my own mother.<sup>18</sup>Even young children despise me; when I rise they talk against me.<sup>19</sup>All my intimate friends abhor me, and those whom I loved have turned against me.<sup>20</sup>My bones stick to my skin and to my flesh, and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.<sup>21</sup>Have mercy on me, have mercy on me, O you my friends, for the hand of God has touched me!<sup>22</sup>Why do you, like God, pursue me? Why are you not satisfied with my flesh?<sup>23</sup>"Oh that my words were written! Oh that they were inscribed in a book!<sup>24</sup>Oh that with an iron pen and lead they were engraved in the rock forever!<sup>25</sup>For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.<sup>26</sup>And after my skin has been thus destroyed, yet in my flesh I shall see God,<sup>27</sup>whom I shall see for myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another. My heart faints within me!<sup>28</sup>If you say, 'How we will pursue him!' and, 'The root of the matter is found in him,'<sup>29</sup>be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment."
19.overview: Job asks how long the friends will torment him; if they use his disgrace as proof of guilt, let them know God has put him in the wrong and closed his net around him (vv. 1-6). He cries Violence! and is not answered; God has walled up his way, stripped his glory, uprooted his hope like a tree, and besieged him as an enemy (vv. 7-12). Brothers, relatives, friends, guests, servants, his wife and even children have turned from him; he has escaped by the skin of his teeth; he begs the friends for pity, for the hand of God has touched him (vv. 13-22). He longs for his words to be engraved in rock: For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth; after his skin is destroyed, in his flesh he will see God with his own eyes. Let the friends fear the sword of judgment (vv. 23-29).
19.theology:
The go'el is the kinsman who redeems the land, the slave and the blood of his relative (Lev 25; Num 35; Ruth 4), and above all it is God's name (Isa 41:14). Isaiah joins Job's Redeemer and last (Isa 44:6), and the risen Christ takes them with the living one (Rev 1:17-18). This is the summit of the book's mediator sequence (9:33; 16:19).

After the destruction of his body Job will see God with his own eyes, and not as a stranger: the hope of the resurrection of the body (1 Cor 15:42-44) and the vision of God (1 John 3:2; Rev 22:4).
19.examples:
Ten times: five speeches, and an idiom.

Violence! and no answer: Habakkuk 1:2.

Stripped of glory, the crown taken: the soldiers and the thorns.

A stranger in his own house: Psalm 69:8.

Oh that my words were written: they were.

Redeemer and last: Isaiah 44:6 and Revelation 1:17-18.

The Redeemer stands on the dust where Job will lie.

Not another: not a stranger.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — How Long Will You Torment Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words? Ten times they have reproached him (vv. 1-3). If he has erred, his error is his own; if they use his disgrace as proof against him, let them know that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me (vv. 4-6).
verseByVerse.theology: Job names what the friends have been doing: using his suffering as evidence. He knows the suffering came from God's hand, not from his own feet walking into a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Job answered and said: "How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words? These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Job answered and said: How long will you torment me and break me in pieces with words? These ten times you have cast reproach upon me; are you not ashamed to wrong me?

Bildad has just told Job that he does not know God (18:21). Job's reply begins in exhaustion: how long? Their words have been like hammers. Ten times is not a count; the friends have spoken five times so far. It is the Hebrew way of saying "over and over again", as Jacob said Laban had changed his wages ten times (Gen 31:7). Job has been reproached so often he has stopped counting.

Are you not ashamed? The friends came to show him sympathy and comfort him (2:11). They have wronged him, and they do not blush. This chapter goes deeper into the dark than any before it, and then climbs higher than any before it. It begins here, with a man broken by the words of his friends.

verseByVerse.quote: And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself. If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me, know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And even if it be true that I have erred, my error remains with myself. Suppose I have sinned somewhere; that is between me and God. It has not harmed you, and it gives you no right to stand over me.

If indeed you magnify yourselves against me and make my disgrace an argument against me, know then that God has put me in the wrong and closed his net about me. Here is exactly what the friends have done: they have taken his disgrace, his ruined body and his dead children, and used it as proof of his guilt. Job says: you have the cause wrong. It was not my sin that did this. It was God.

Listen to the two words he chooses. Put me in the wrong is the verb of Bildad's first question, Does God pervert justice? (8:3). And his net answers Bildad's last speech, where the wicked man is cast into a net by his own feet (18:8). No, says Job, I did not walk into this. It was God who spread the net. He is right that God's hand is in it (2:3). He is wrong, and will be told so, to think God has done him wrong (40:8).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–12 — He Has Walled Up My Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: I cry out, Violence! but I am not answered (v. 7). God has walled up his way and darkened his paths (v. 8), stripped him of his glory and taken the crown from his head (v. 9), torn him down and uprooted his hope like a tree (v. 10), and counts him an enemy, laying siege to his tent (vv. 11-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Job's picture of God is still of an enemy besieging him. It will not stay that way to the end of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I cry out, 'Violence!' but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice. He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass, and he has set darkness upon my paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Behold, I cry out, Violence! but I am not answered; I call for help, but there is no justice.

A man attacked in the street shouts for help, and no one comes. Job shouts "Violence!" at heaven and hears nothing.
